docs.title: 📌 What is Data Analytics?
docs.text:
Data Analytics is the process of: - Collecting - Cleaning - Organizing - Analyzing data

With the goal of: - Discovering useful information - Drawing conclusions - Supporting decision-making

docs.title: 🔍 Types of Data Analytics
docs.text:
1. Descriptive Analytics
  2. Answers: What happened?

  3. Example: Sales reports, website traffic summaries.

  4. Diagnostic Analytics

  5. Answers: Why did it happen?

  6. Example: Root cause analysis of low sales.

  7. Predictive Analytics

  8. Answers: What is likely to happen?

  9. Example: Forecasting sales using historical data.

  10. Prescriptive Analytics

  11. Answers: What should be done?
  12. Example: Recommending actions using AI and machine learning.

docs.title: 🧰 Key Components
docs.text:
• Data Collection: Gathering data from various sources (surveys, sensors, logs, databases, APIs).
  • Data Cleaning: Removing errors, handling missing data, and formatting.
  • Data Exploration: Using statistics and visualizations to understand patterns.
  • Data Analysis: Applying techniques (e.g., regression, clustering).
  • Data Visualization: Creating charts and dashboards using tools like Power BI, Tableau, or Python libraries (Matplotlib, Seaborn).

docs.title: 🧠 Skills Required
docs.text:
• Statistics & Mathematics
  • Data Manipulation (e.g., SQL, Excel, Pandas)
  • Data Visualization
  • Programming (Python, R)
  • Machine Learning (for advanced analytics)

docs.title: 1. 🔗 Azure DevOps
docs.text:
Azure covers a wide range of services — from hosting web apps and APIs to managing databases, CI/CD pipelines, machine learning, virtual machines, and more.

Azure DevOps is a powerful platform for managing the entire software development lifecycle — including version control (Git), CI/CD pipelines, project tracking, testing, and artifact management.

docs.title: 🔧 Core Services in Azure DevOps:
docs.text: Service Description Azure Boards Work item tracking (Agile, Scrum, Kanban). Azure Repos Git repositories for source code. Azure Pipelines Build and release pipelines (CI/CD). Azure Test Plans Manual and exploratory testing tools. Azure Artifacts Package management (NuGet, npm, Maven, etc.).

docs.title: 🗂️ Azure DevOps Work Process (for Boards)
docs.text:
Choose a process template to define how teams interact within the Azure DevOps framework:

Template Description Basic Simplest model using Issues, Tasks, and Epics. Agile Supports Agile planning and tracks dev/test separately. Scrum Track PBIs and bugs on Kanban, break into tasks on taskboard. CMMI Supports formal change management and work tracking.

docs.text:
Build pipeline: • these pipelines jobs clone the code from assigned repositories and build the project based on instruction provided in yaml file. • Typically, we use build pipeline to publish artifacts of the project • Based on instruction we can build any kind of project like .net, JavaScript, angular etc.

Release Pipeline: • These pipelines generally used to deploy the build artifacts into agent Machines.

Create Release: • This component helps us to build end to end pipeline (connecting build and release pipeline) For CI/CD implementation.

docs.title: Azure Test Plans:
docs.text: It is a service in Azure DevOps used for manual testing, exploratory testing, and user acceptance testing (UAT). It helps teams plan, track, and manage testing efforts across the DevOps lifecycle.

docs.title: Advance Features:
docs.text:
✅ Test Configurations: Run the same test on different environments (e.g., OS, browsers).

🔗 Work Item Integration: Link test cases to requirements and bugs.

📈 Reporting & Analytics: Use built-in Power BI integrations for test analytics.

🧪 Automated Test Integration: You can link automated tests from pipelines to test plans (e.g., via .runsettings or TestCase attributes in code).

docs.title: Create Azure Tests:
docs.text:
1. Create a Test Plan

Go to Azure DevOps > Test Plans.

  1. Click + New Test Plan.

  2. Add Test Suites

    • Static Suite: Manually add test cases.

    • Requirement-based Suite: Linked to backlog items (e.g., user stories).

    • Query-based Suite: Dynamically pulls test cases from a work item query.

  3. Create Test Cases

    • Add steps with expected results.

    • Attach screenshots, files, or links if needed.

  4. Run Tests

    • Click Run for web application or use the Test Runner.

    • Mark each step as pass/fail during execution.

    • Automatically create bugs when a step fails.

  5. Track Results

    • View Run summary, including test outcomes and execution time.

    • Use dashboards and reports to analyze quality

docs.title: Different way of deploying the Web Application on Azure
1. Deploying the Web app using Azure App service
docs.text:
I am going to use the command window / cloud cell here

  1. Define the web app name
webappname="DevOpsSolution"
  1. Create an App service plan in S1 tier
az appservice plan create --name $webappname --resource-group learn-50ccdcdf-3e51-4ea3-8084-44bb6a213df2 --sku S1
  1. Create the web app resources using the App service plan in same resource group
az webapp create --name $webappname --resource-group learn-35e59348-a05b-4105-9fd0-88fab98e170d --plan $webappname
  1. Set the deployment branch to main in the appsettings configuratioon.
az webapp config appsettings set --name $webappname --resource-group learn-35e59348-a05b-4105-9fd0-88fab98e170d --setting DEPLOYMENT_BRANCH=main
  1. Set the deployment credentials
az webapp deployment user set --user-name UsrXYZ --password Pass@xyz
  1. Configure the web app to accept deployments from local git and display the git deployment URL: 
echo Git deployment URL :$(az webapp deployment source config-local-git --name $webappname --resource-group learn-35e59348-a05b-4105-9fd0-88fab98e170d --query url --output tsv)

or 

echo Git deployment https://github.com/Abhikpt/DevOpsSolution :$(az webapp deployment source config-local-git --name $webappname --resource-group learn-35e59348-a05b-4105-9fd0-88fab98e170d --query url --output tsv)
  1. Display the web app URL
echo Web app URL: http://$webappname.azurewebsite.net

  1. Now go to you local command terminal

  2. add the Remote URL (point 06) to local repository

git remote add azure-prod GIT_DEPLOYMENT_URL
  • push the local default branch main to azure-prod
git push azure-prod main

  • wait till get get success response of deployment

  • Open the Web App URL (point 07) and check app has been built and deployed.

docs.title: 📒 CI/CD for Playwright with C# and NUnit (GitHub Actions)
✅ Project Structure (Relevant for CI)
docs.text:
/TestResults/               <-- NUnit test result (.trx)
/Screenshot/                <-- Screenshots (e.g., failed tests)
/Resources/                 <-- HTML reports (Playwright)
/Logs/                      <-- Optional: custom log files
/bin/Release/net8.0/        <-- Compiled binaries and playwright.ps1

docs.title: 📁 Location:
docs.text: .github/workflows/playwright.yml

docs.title: 📋 Trigger:
docs.text:
Runs on every push to the main branch:

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

docs.title: 🛠 Full Example Workflow with Explanation
docs.text:
name: Playwright Test Workflow

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - project_ql

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Check out the code
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up .NET SDK
      - name: Set up .NET
        uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with:
          dotnet-version: '8.0'

      # Restore dependencies
      - name: Restore dependencies
        run: dotnet restore

      # Build project
      - name: Build project
        run: dotnet build --configuration Release --no-restore

      # adding this steps to debug the correct path
      - name: List Playwright script path
        run: ls -R bin/

      - name: Install Playwright Browsers
        run: pwsh bin/Release/net8.0/playwright.ps1 install  # adjust net version

       # 👉 Add this step to run tests with xvfb (for headed mode)
      - name: Run Playwright Tests
        run: xvfb-run -a dotnet test --configuration Release --no-build --logger "trx;LogFileName=test-results.trx"

      # Upload artifacts
      - name: Upload test-logs
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: test-logs
          path: |
            TestResults/
            Logs/ 
            Screenshots/
            Resources/
            bin/Debug/net8.0/playwright-report/
  download_artifacts:
    needs: build  # Ensure this job runs after the 'build' job
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Download uploaded artifacts
      - name: Download test-logs artifact
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: test-logs
          path: ./downloaded-artifacts

docs.title: ✅ Step 1: Checkout Code
docs.text:
- name: Checkout code
  uses: actions/checkout@v3
  • Pulls the code from your GitHub repository into the runner machine.

docs.title: ✅ Step 2: Setup .NET SDK
docs.text:
- name: Setup .NET
  uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v3
  with:
    dotnet-version: '8.0'
  • Installs the .NET 8 SDK so we can build and test our C# Playwright project.

docs.title: ✅ Step 3: Restore NuGet Packages
docs.text:
- name: Restore dependencies
  run: dotnet restore
  • Restores all dependencies defined in your .csproj files using NuGet.

docs.title: ✅ Step 4: Build the Project
docs.text:
- name: Build project
  run: dotnet build --configuration Release --no-restore
  • Compiles the code in Release mode.
  • --no-restore skips restoring packages again (already done in the previous step).

docs.title: ✅ Step 5: Install Playwright Browsers
docs.text:
- name: Install Playwright Browsers
  run: pwsh bin/Release/net8.0/playwright.ps1 install
  • Installs the required browsers (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) via Playwright.
  • This script is auto-generated after building the project.

docs.title: ✅ Step 6: Run Tests (With xvfb for UI Support)
docs.text:
- name: Run Playwright Tests (headful mode with xvfb)
  run: xvfb-run -a dotnet test --configuration Release --no-build --logger "trx;LogFileName=test-results.trx"
  • Runs NUnit tests.
  • xvfb-run is used to simulate a display environment for UI browsers. ie. headed mode of browser.
  • --logger "trx" generates a test result file.

docs.title: ✅ Step 7: Upload Test Artifacts
docs.text:
- name: Upload test artifacts
  if: always()
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
  with:
    name: test-results
    path: |
      TestResults/
      Screenshot/
      Resources/
      Logs/
  • Uploads results (screenshots, reports, logs) for review, even if tests fail.
  • You can later download these artifacts from the GitHub Actions UI.

docs.title: ✅ Step 8: Download Artifacts (Optional Step)
docs.text:
- name: Download test artifacts
  uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
  with:
    name: test-results
  • Allows retrieval of uploaded test artifacts in subsequent jobs or local machine.
  • Useful for report parsing, publishing, or retention.

docs.title: 🧠 Summary of Tools Used
docs.text: Tool Purpose dotnet CLI Build, restore, test C# projects playwright.ps1 install Installs browser dependencies xvfb-run Provides virtual display for UI browser runs upload-artifact Saves screenshots, logs, test results for download download-artifact Retrieves uploaded files for further use in pipeline or local

docs.title: 💡 Tips
docs.text:
• Use if: always() when uploading artifacts — ensures logs/screenshots are saved even on test failure.
  • Use xvfb-run only when running Playwright in headed mode (browser UI). Otherwise, set Headless = true in test code.
  • Always confirm your output folders (e.g., Screenshot/, Resources/) exist before uploading them.
  • Download artifacts in separate jobs if you plan to analyze or publish reports further.

docs.title: 📁 What is Git?
docs.text: Git is a: - Free - Open-source - Distributed - Version Control System (VCS) - Designed to handle everything from small to large projects with speed and efficiency. - Git allows you to have local repositories.

docs.title: Git commands:
docs.text:
🔹 1. Branch Basics

  • View branches
git branch        # local branches
git branch -r     # remote branches
git branch -a     # all branches
  • Create branch
git checkout -b feature/uat3
  • Switch branch
git checkout develop
  • Rename branch
git branch -m old-name new-name

🔹 2. Staging, Changes & Commits

  • Changes → modified but not yet staged.

  • Staged changes → added via git add, waiting for commit.

  • Commit changes:

git commit -m "message"
  • Unstage files:
git reset HEAD <file>
  • Check staged/unstaged:
git status

🔹 3. See Changed Files (diffs)

3.1 Changed file names only - Compare working dir vs last commit:

git diff --name-only
  • Compare two commits:
git diff --name-only <commit1> <commit2>
  • Compare staged changes:
git diff --name-only --cached
  • Compare last commit:
git diff --name-only HEAD~1 HEAD
  • Show status (added/modified/deleted):
git diff --name-status

3.2 Changes in a specific file

  • Working directory:
git diff <file-path>
  • Staged changes:
git diff --cached <file-path>
  • Between commits:
git diff <commit1> <commit2> -- <file-path>
  • File name only:
git diff --name-only -- <file-path>

🔹 4. Stash

Temporarily saves your changes without committing.

  • Save changes:
git stash
  • Apply stashed changes:
git stash pop
  • Apply later (keep stash):
git stash apply
  • View stashes:
git stash list

👉 You can stash in any branch, then apply in another branch.

🔹 5. Push

  • Push current branch
git push

✅ Only current branch is pushed (0% chance others get pushed).

Push specific branch

git push origin feature/login

-Push all branches (⚠ risky)

git push --all
  • Check before push
git push --dry-run

🔹 6. Revert, Reset & Push

  • Revert (safe, shared branches)
git revert <commit-id>
git push origin <branch>
  • If branch is behind remote
git pull --rebase origin <branch>
git push origin <branch>
  • Reset (rewrite history, risky)
git reset --hard <commit-id>
git push origin branch-name --force

🔹 7. Remove Branch & Fetch from Remote

  • Switch to another branch:
git checkout main
  • Delete local branch:
git branch -D <branch>
  • Fetch remote:
git fetch origin
  • Recreate from remote:
git checkout -b <branch> origin/<branch>

🔹 8. Compare Branches

  • Full diff:
git diff staging origin/develop
  • File names only:
git diff --name-only staging origin/develop
  • Summary:
git diff --stat staging origin/develop
  • Commits in staging but not develop:
git log origin/develop..staging --oneline
  • Commits in develop but not staging:
git log staging..origin/develop --oneline

🔹 9. Fix “Your branch and 'origin/branch' have diverged”

  • Merge (keep both histories)
git fetch origin
git checkout <branch>
git merge origin/<branch>
git push origin <branch>
  • Rebase (clean history)
git fetch origin
git checkout <branch>
git rebase origin/<branch>
git push origin <branch> --force-with-lease
  • Reset (discard local commits)
git fetch origin
git checkout <branch>
git reset --hard origin/<branch>

🔹 10. Merge vs Rebase

  • Merge
git merge develop

Keeps history (adds merge commit). Safe for teamwork.

  • Rebase
git rebase develop

Replays commits on new base. Cleaner history, risky if branch is already pushed.

🔹 11. Conflicts

  • During merge/rebase, Git stops at conflicts.
git status   # shows conflicts
git add <file>
git merge --continue   # or git rebase --continue
  • Abort rebase:
git rebase --abort

🔹 12. Git Config

  • Check config
git config --list
  • Set global username/email
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
  • Set per-repo
git config user.name "Your Name"
git config user.email "you@example.com"

🔹 13. Delete Files

  • Delete file + folder:
git rm -r foldername
git commit -m "remove folder"
git push

🔹 14. History

  • View commit history:
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
  • Show details:
git show <commit-id>

🔹 15. Sync with Remote

  • Fetch updates
git fetch origin
  • Merge develop into your branch
git checkout fixes
git merge origin/develop
  • Rebase instead
git checkout fixes
git rebase origin/develop

🔹 16. Rebase Interactive

git rebase -i HEAD~3
  • Options:
pick → keep
squash → combine
edit → modify
drop → remove

🔹 17. Undo Push (Remote)

  • If safe (personal branch)
git reset --hard <commit-id>
git push origin branch --force
  • If shared branch
git revert <commit-id>
git push origin branch

✅ Golden Rules

  • Use merge for team branches (safe).
  • Use rebase/reset only for your own branch before pushing.
  • Use revert to safely undo in shared repos.
  • Always git pull --rebase before pushing if behind.

docs.title: Working with SSH key:
docs.text:
It is an secure Authentication methodused to connect youer local maching like git bash to remote services like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket.

  • You can access and write data in repositories on GitHub using SSH (Secure Shell Protocol).
  • When you connect via SSH, you authenticate using a private key file on your local machine.

🔐 Step 1: Generate an SSH key 1. Open Git Bash/ Git CMD (Search for it in the Start menu). 2. Run this command to create a new key:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
  1. Replace "your_email@example.com" with your actual email (used for GitHub, GitLab, etc.).
  2. If ed25519 doesn’t work, try rsa with:
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"
  1. When prompted:
Enter file in which to save the key (/c/Users/YourName/.ssh/id_ed25519):
Press Enter to accept the default.
  1. Enter a passphrase (optional, for security), or just press Enter to skip.

🧠 Step 2: Start ssh-agent and add the key 1. In Git Bash, run:

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
  1. Then add your SSH key to the agent:
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  1. You should see a confirmation like:
Identity added: /c/Users/YourName/.ssh/id_ed25519

📋 Step 3: Copy your public key To copy the public key:

clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

This copies your SSH public key to the clipboard.

☁️ Step 4: Add your key to GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket - GitHub: https://github.com/settings/keys - GitLab: https://gitlab.com/profile/keys - Bitbucket: https://bitbucket.org/account/settings/ssh-keys/

Click New SSH Key, give it a name, paste your key in, and save.

🔁 Step 5: Test the connection

  • To test GitHub, run:
ssh -T git@github.com
  • Expected response:
Hi yourusername! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.

docs.title: how to clone an private repository:
1.  Using HTTPS with Personal Access Token (PAT)
docs.text:
If you're using GitHub (similar steps for GitLab, Bitbucket):

🔹 Steps: a. Go to the repository page. b. Click on "Code" → Select HTTPS → Copy the URL. c.Run:

git clone https://github.com/username/repo-name.git

d. When prompted:

  • Username → Enter your GitHub username.
  • Password → Enter your Personal Access Token (PAT) (not your GitHub password).

e. GitHub no longer supports password authentication for Git over HTTPS. You must use a token.

🔹 Generate a PAT:
GitHub: https://github.com/settings/tokens
GitLab: https://gitlab.com/-/profile/personal_access_tokens

docs.title: 2. Using SSH (Recommended for frequent access)
docs.text:
a. Generate SSH Key (if not done already):

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

b. Add SSH key to your GitHub/GitLab account:

docs.title: Basics of deployment:
docs.text: Application deployment is the process of making an application available for users to access and use. It involves transferring the built application from the development environment to a server or cloud platform where it can be run and accessed by users. Here’s a basic overview of the deployment process:

docs.title: 1.  Understand the Types of Deployment
docs.text: • Manual Deployment: The developer manually copies application files to the target server and configures the necessary settings. This method is more error-prone but is suitable for simple applications. • Automated Deployment: Tools like Jenkins, GitHub Actions, or Azure DevOps automate the deployment process to minimize errors and improve efficiency.

docs.title: 2.  Deployment Environments
docs.text: Applications are deployed to different environments for different purposes: • Development Environment: Used by developers to code and test new features. • Testing/Staging Environment: A replica of production where QA can test the application before it goes live. • Production Environment: The live environment accessible by end-users.

docs.title: 3.  Deployment Steps
docs.text:
Here are the typical steps involved in deploying an application:

a. Build the Application • Build Process: Compile the source code into a format that can be run by a server (e.g., an executable or a set of static files). • Package: Bundle the built application into a package or an archive (e.g., .zip, .tar, .war, .dll).

b. Prepare the Target Server • Provisioning: Set up the server (physical or virtual) where the application will run. This could be a dedicated server, a cloud instance, or a container. • Configure Dependencies: Install necessary dependencies such as runtimes (e.g., .NET Core, Java, Node.js), libraries, and other services the application needs.

c. Transfer Files • Transfer the built files to the target server using tools like: o FTP/SFTP: For file transfer between local machines and remote servers. o SSH: Secure shell for accessing servers and copying files (scp). o Deployment Tools: Tools like rsync, Ansible, or container registries for Docker images.

d. Configuration • Environment-Specific Configurations: Set environment-specific configurations, such as database connection strings, API keys, etc. • Environment Variables: Use environment variables to avoid hard-coding sensitive information in your codebase.

e. Start the Application • Web Servers: Deploy the application to a web server like Apache, NGINX, IIS, or Kestrel for serving HTTP requests. • Containers: Deploy as Docker containers using Docker Compose or orchestration tools like Kubernetes. • Cloud Services: Deploy to cloud services like Azure App Service, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, or Google App Engine for easy scaling and management.

f. Monitoring & Testing • Smoke Testing: After deployment, perform basic tests to ensure the application is running correctly. • Monitoring: Set up monitoring for your application to track uptime, performance, and errors. Tools like Prometheus, Grafana, or cloud-native monitoring solutions can help.

docs.title: 4.  Deployment Models
docs.text: • Rolling Deployment: Gradually update parts of the application so that there is no downtime. This helps ensure that users still have access during the update. • Blue-Green Deployment: Set up two identical environments (blue and green). Deploy to one environment, and if everything works fine, switch traffic from the old environment to the new one. • Canary Deployment: Roll out the new version to a small subset of users first before a full-scale rollout. This approach helps minimize the impact of potential issues.

docs.title: 5.  CI/CD in Deployment
docs.text: • Continuous Integration (CI): Automatically build and test code changes whenever developers push code to version control. • Continuous Deployment (CD): Automatically deploy changes that pass tests to the production environment. This provides a seamless flow from development to production.

docs.title: 6.  Deployment Tools
docs.text: • Jenkins: Automate build, test, and deployment processes. • GitHub Actions: Run workflows to build, test, and deploy directly from GitHub. • Docker: Containerize applications for easy deployment across different environments. • Kubernetes: Automate deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. • Ansible/Chef/Puppet: Automate server setup, configuration, and deployment.

docs.title: Application / Software server vs Servers:
docs.text: Application servers are specialized software that provides an environment for applications to run, manage business logic, and facilitate communication between the client and the database or backend services.

docs.title: Application Server Options by Language
docs.text: This document provides an overview of common application server options based on programming language, along with their descriptions and typical use cases.

docs.title: C
docs.text: Application Server Description and Use Cases Kestrel Default ASP.NET Core server, often used with Nginx/Apache as a reverse proxy. IIS Enterprise server for Windows environments. Azure App Service Managed cloud hosting for .NET apps. NGINX/Apache with Kestrel Reverse proxy for handling traffic, SSL, and load balancing.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: Application Server Description and Use Cases Gunicorn WSGI server for Flask, Django, etc., often with NGINX. uWSGI Flexible WSGI server paired with NGINX for scalability. Apache HTTP Server with mod_wsgi Hosts Python web applications using Apache. Daphne Used for real-time Django applications.

docs.title: Java
docs.text: Application Server Description and Use Cases Apache Tomcat Lightweight, popular for JSP/Servlet applications. WildFly Java EE application server for enterprise-grade apps. Apache TomEE Tomcat with Java EE capabilities. GlassFish Full Java EE server, good for development and testing. Jetty Lightweight, ideal for embedded or microservices deployment.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Actual servers are the physical or virtual machines that host these application servers, providing the necessary infrastructure and resources for applications to operate.

docs.text:
Basic steps to create a running application is: 1. Create the project  2. Build the project  dotnet build or (dotnet publish -c release -o ./publish) 3. Deployed the project on server to run it  copy the build file and placed in server path like tomcat server or local server

CI (Continuous Integration): Continuous Integration is the practice of frequently integrating code changes into a shared repository. Each integration is verified by automated builds and tests to detect issues early in the development process. Key Features: 1. Frequent Commits: Developers commit code changes regularly (multiple times a day) to the shared repository. 2. Automated Builds: Each commit triggers an automated build process, compiling the code to ensure it can be built without errors. 3. Automated Testing: Automated tests (unit tests, integration tests) are executed to verify that the new code does not break existing functionality. 4. Immediate Feedback: Developers receive quick feedback on the success or failure of their changes, allowing for prompt bug fixes.

docs.title: CD (Continuous delivery):
docs.text: Continuous Deployment takes Continuous integration a step further by automatically deploying every change that passes automated testing directly to production without manual intervention. Key Features: 1. No Manual Approval: Changes are deployed to production automatically once they pass the testing phase. 2. Frequent Releases: The application can be updated multiple times a day, enabling rapid delivery of new features, improvements, and fixes. 3. Monitoring and Rollback: Continuous deployment typically includes monitoring and rollback mechanisms to quickly address any issues that arise in production.

docs.title: Building CI with Azure pipelines:
docs.text: • Azure Pipelines is a cloud-based service provided by Microsoft Azure that enables you to automate the building, testing, and deployment of your applications. • It is a key component of Azure DevOps, which provides a comprehensive set of development tools and services for managing the entire software development lifecycle. • Azure Pipelines supports various programming languages, platforms, and cloud environments, making it a versatile choice for CI/CD practices.

docs.title: Key Features of Azure Pipelines
docs.text:
1. Continuous Integration (CI): o Automate the building and testing of code changes when they are pushed to a version control system (like GitHub, Azure Repos, etc.). o Supports various build agents, including Windows, Linux, and macOS.
  2. Continuous Deployment (CD): o Automatically deploy applications to various environments (development, testing, production) based on defined triggers and conditions. o Integrates with Azure services and third-party services for seamless deployment.
  3. Multi-Platform Support: o Supports a wide range of programming languages, including .NET, Java, Python, Node.js, and more. o Can deploy applications to various platforms such as Azure App Services, Kubernetes, virtual machines, and other cloud services.
  4. Pipeline as Code: o Define your CI/CD pipeline using YAML configuration files, allowing versioning and easier management of your pipeline configuration. o YAML pipelines provide a more flexible and powerful way to define the build and release process.
  5. Integration with Other Tools: o Integrates seamlessly with Azure DevOps Services, GitHub, Docker, Jenkins, and other tools and services, allowing for a more robust development workflow. o Supports the use of custom tasks and extensions to enhance the pipeline capabilities.
  6. Multi-Stage Pipelines: o Support for creating multi-stage pipelines, allowing you to define various stages (build, test, deploy) in a single YAML file. o Enables complex workflows with conditions and approvals between stages.
  7. Environment Management: o Manage deployment environments directly within Azure Pipelines, allowing you to define different configurations and approvals for production deployments.

docs.title: Azure Pipelines:
docs.text:
Build pipeline: • these pipelines jobs clone the code from assigned repositories and build the project based on instruction provided in yaml file. • Typically, we use build pipeline to publish artifacts of the project • Based on instruction we can build any kind of project like .net, JavaScript, angular etc.

Release Pipeline: • These pipelines generally used to deploy the build artifacts into agent Machines.

Create Release: • This component helps us to build end to end pipeline (connecting build and release pipeline) For CI/CD implementation.

docs.title: Basic terms / tool on ADO board:
docs.text:
1. Pipeline: A definition of the steps needed to build, test, and deploy your application. Can be defined in the Azure DevOps portal or through a YAML file.
  2. Build Pipeline: Automates the build process, including compiling code, running tests, and packaging the application.
  3. Release Pipeline: Automates the deployment of applications to various environments.
  4. Agent: A software component that runs the tasks in your pipeline. Azure provides hosted agents, or you can set up self-hosted agents.
  5. Task: A single unit of work that does something, like compiling code or running tests.

docs.title: Setting Up Azure Pipelines
docs.text:
1. Create an Azure DevOps Organization: o Go to the Azure DevOps website and create a new organization if you don't have one.
  2. Create a New Project: o Within your Azure DevOps organization, create a new project to house your pipeline.
  3. Create a Pipeline: o Go to the Pipelines section and select "New Pipeline." o Follow the wizard to connect your repository (e.g., GitHub, Azure Repos) and select the YAML file or configure your pipeline.
  4. Run the Pipeline: o Once the pipeline is created, you can manually trigger it or let it run automatically based on the defined triggers.

docs.title: Example of a Basic YAML Pipeline
docs.text:
Here’s a simple example of a YAML pipeline that builds a .NET application:

trigger:
  - main

pool:
  vmImage: 'windows-latest'

steps:
- task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
  inputs:
    command: 'build'
    projects: '**/*.csproj'
    versioningScheme: 'byBuildNumber'
    publishWebProjects: true

- task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
  inputs:
    command: 'test'
    projects: '**/*.csproj'

docs.title: Breakdown of the YAML Pipeline
docs.text:
1. trigger: Defines the branch that triggers the pipeline. In this case, it triggers on the main branch.
  2. pool: Specifies the type of agent to use. Here, it uses a hosted Windows agent.
  3. steps: Lists the tasks to be executed in the pipeline: o The first task uses the DotNetCoreCLI task to build all .csproj projects. o The second task runs tests on all .csproj projects.

docs.title: Hosting a static Website on GitHub:
docs.text:
1. Create a GitHub account on github.com.
  2. Download either GitHub for Mac or GitHub for Windows, depending on your operating system. Open the app and log in using the account you just created.
  3. (On Mac): After you login, click advanced and make sure that your name and email are correct. Then, click "Install Command Line Tools", just in case you want to start using the command line later in life.
  4. Create a new repository in your GitHub application. Name it your-username.github.io. The name is very important. Note the folder that GitHub is saving the repository to. Make sure the "Push to GitHub?" box is checked.
  5. Move your website's files into the folder that GitHub just created when you made the repository. IMPORTANT: Your homepage HTML file must be called "index.html", and it must exist in the top-level directory.
  6. Back in the GitHub application, you should see your files in the left column. Make sure they are all checked. If so, enter a message in the text box called "commit summary", something like "initial commit." Then, click the commit button.
  7. Click the "Publish repo" button in the top right corner.
  8. Give it about 10 minutes, then check your-username.github.io. Your website should be there!

docs.title: Publish blazer App on GitHub;
docs.text:
• Deployed using GitHub Action • Create workflow • Main.yml file

name: Deploy blazor app to GitHub Pages

# Run workflow on every push to the master branch
on:
  push:
    branches: [master]

jobs:
  deploy-to-github-pages:
    # use ubuntu-latest image to run steps on
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    # uses GitHub's checkout action to checkout code form the master branch
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2

    # Setup .NET Core SDK 3.1
    - name: Setup .NET Core SDK
      uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v1
      with:
        dotnet-version: 6.x
        include-prerelease: true

    # publishes Blazor project to the release-folder
    - name: Publish .NET Core Project
      run: dotnet publish LearningwithAbhi.sln -c Release -o release --nologo

    # changes the base-tag in index.html from '/' to 'LearningwithAbhi' to match GitHub Pages repository subdirectory
    - name: Change base-tag in index.html from / to LearningwithAbhi
      run: sed -i 's/<base href="\/" \/>/<base href="\/LearningwithAbhi\/" \/>/g' release/wwwroot/index.html

    # copy index.html to 404.html to serve the same file when a file is not found
    - name: copy index.html to 404.html
      run: cp release/wwwroot/index.html release/wwwroot/404.html

    # add .nojekyll file to tell GitHub pages to not treat this as a Jekyll project. (Allow files and folders starting with an underscore)
    - name: Add .nojekyll file
      run: touch release/wwwroot/.nojekyll

    - name: Commit wwwroot to GitHub Pages
      uses: JamesIves/github-pages-deploy-action@3.7.1
      with:
        GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        BRANCH: gh-pages
        FOLDER: release/wwwroot

To create a Docker image, you generally need a Dockerfile that contains a set of instructions Docker uses to build the image. - Create a Dockerfile

docker build -t myapp:latest .

docs.title: Creating docker container
docs.text:
A container is a running instance of a Docker image. To create one, you use the docker run command.

Syntax: docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE [COMMAND] [ARG...]

Options: -d -> Run in background -i -> Attach input -t -> Attach output --name NAME -> Name container --entrypoint=/bin/bash -> Override entrypoint -p 8080:8080 -> Map ports -v /host:/container -> Volume mapping

Example:

# 1.Runs the container in detached mode
docker run -d imageName

# 2.Runs the ubuntu container in interactive mode with terminal access
docker run -it ubuntu 

# 3.Runs the container with custom entrypoint (e.g., bash)
docker run -it --entrypoint=/bin/bash imageName

# 4.Run a container with mounted volume
docker run -d -v /host/path:/container/path myimage

# 5.Remove container
docker rm containerName

docs.title: Port Mapping in Docker
docs.text:
Port Mapping is a technique used to allow communication between devices or applications by mapping ports on a host machine to specific ports on another machine or a containerized environment. It's commonly used in networking, containerization (e.g., Docker), and application hosting.

  • If multiple applications are running on a machine, then to access them from external applications/machines we use port mapping.
  • At a time two applications cannot be assigned the same port. We have to stop one application to assign the port to another.

docs.title: Why is Port Mapping Needed?
docs.text:
1. External Access: Makes an application or service running on a specific port inside a container or a private network accessible externally.
  2. Port Collision Avoidance: Helps to avoid conflicts when multiple services use the same port.
  3. Control and Security: Restricts access to specific ports and provides flexibility in managing traffic.

docs.title: Docker Command for Port Mapping
docs.text:
docker run -p hostPort:containerPort image
  • Port 80 is the default port.

docs.title: Examples:
docs.text:
docker run -p 80:80 vindocker/jmserver
docker run -p 4444:80 mongo
  • Docker Multi-Container Flow (with Network and Host Access)
                ┌────────────┐
                │ Machine A  │
                └─────┬──────┘
                      │
               10.11.12.13
                      │
                      ▼
            ┌────────────────────┐
            │      Docker        │
            ├────────┬───────────┤
            │ Port 80│ Port 90   │
            ├────────┴───────────┤
            │                    │
  ┌───────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
  │ Container/vm 1│   │ Container/vm 2 │
  │───────────────│   │────────────────│
  │ Jenkins   :80 │   │ MongoDB   :90  │
  │ Ubuntu    :9023│  │ Selenium  :80  │
  └───────────────┘   └────────────────┘
  • For the above scenario, port mappings will be:
docker run -p 80:80 vindocker/jenkins
docker run -p 80:9023 vindocker/Ubuntu
docker run -p 90:80 SeleniumGrid

docs.title: Dockerfile:
docs.text:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:6.0 AS base
WORKDIR /app
EXPOSE 80
EXPOSE 443

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:6.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["GraphQL.NET/GraphQLProductApp.csproj", "GraphQL.NET/"]
RUN dotnet restore "GraphQL.NET/GraphQLProductApp.csproj"
COPY . .
WORKDIR "/src/GraphQL.NET"
RUN dotnet build "GraphQLProductApp.csproj" -c Release -o /app/build

FROM build AS publish
RUN dotnet publish "GraphQLProductApp.csproj" -c Release -o /app/publish /p:UseAppHost=false

FROM base AS final
ENV ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://*:8000
EXPOSE 8000
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=publish /app/publish .
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "GraphQLProductApp.dll"]

docs.title: Docker Container:
docs.text: Command Description docker ps List all running Docker containers. docker ps -a List all containers, including stopped ones. docker run <image_name> Run a container from a Docker image. docker start <container_id_or_name> Start a stopped container. docker stop <container_id_or_name> Stop a running container. docker restart <container_id_or_name> Restart a container. docker rm <container_id_or_name> Remove a stopped container. docker logs <container_id_or_name> View logs of a container. docker system prune -f Remove stopped containers docker system prune -a Remove stopped + unused images

docs.title: Building Docker Images:
docs.text: • docker build -t <image_name> <path_to_dockerfile> – Build a Docker image from a Dockerfile.

docs.title: Docker Volumes:
docs.text:
• docker volume create <volume_name> – Create a Docker volume.
  • docker volume ls – List all Docker volumes.
  • docker volume rm <volume_name> – Remove a Docker volume.

docs.title: Docker Networks:
docs.text:
• docker network ls – List all Docker networks.
  • docker network create <network_name> – Create a custom Docker network.
  • docker network connect <network_name> <container_name> – Connect a container to a network.

docs.title: Copying Files:
docs.text:
• docker cp <container_id>:<container_path> <host_path> – Copy from container to host.
  • docker cp <host_path> <container_id>:<container_path> – Copy from host to container.

docs.title: Docker-Compose
docs.text:
• docker-compose is a tool for defining and managing multi-container Docker applications.
  • Uses docker-compose.yml to configure services, networks, and volumes.
  • Simplifies running applications requiring multiple containers.

docs.title: Basic Workflow with docker-compose:
docs.text:
1. Define your services in docker-compose.yml.
  2. Run docker-compose up to start services.
  3. Run docker-compose down to stop and clean up.

docs.title: Sample docker-compose.yml Structure:
docs.text:
version: '3'
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    volumes:
      - ./html:/usr/share/nginx/html

  db:
    image: mysql:5.7
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: example
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/mysql

volumes:
  db_data:

docs.title: Understanding the Importance of Pitching
docs.text:
Having a great mobile app idea is just the beginning. To turn it into reality, you need to successfully pitch your idea to potential investors.

Investors need to know: - The problems your app will solve - The value it brings to users - How it will generate revenue

Mastering the pitch is crucial, not only for securing funding but also for effectively introducing your app to the world.

docs.title: Identify the Problem and Target Audience
Identify Your Target Group
docs.text:
Defining your target audience is key. Consider: - Demographics: Age, gender, occupation, location, marital status, education, etc. - Platform preference: Android or iOS? - Socioeconomic status: Are they affluent, middle-class, or budget-conscious?

Being specific helps investors see the potential market clearly.

docs.title: Ask Questions
docs.text:
Engage with your target audience through: - Surveys & Social Media – Gather insights from potential users - Friends & Family – Their perspectives can be invaluable - Online Communities – Find discussions about similar app ideas

Listening to feedback helps uncover hidden problems and opportunities.

docs.title: Analyze the Problem
docs.text:
Ask yourself: - How severe is the problem? - How often does it occur? - What’s causing it? - Has anyone else tried solving it?

Understanding these aspects strengthens your pitch.

docs.title: Define the Solution
docs.text: Focus on solving one or two core problems effectively rather than trying to fix everything at once.

docs.title: Know the Competition
docs.text:
Study your competitors to identify their strengths and weaknesses. Analyze: - Their app design - Marketing strategies - Revenue models - Areas where they fall short

This will help you position your app as a superior solution.

docs.title: Market Validation
docs.text:
Before pitching to investors, ensure there’s a market for your app by gathering data on: - Market size and past growth trends - Number of potential users/customers - Revenue projections and cost of user acquisition

Reliable market research is key to proving your app’s potential profitability.

docs.title: Free vs. Paid Apps
docs.text:
• Paid Apps: Users pay upfront to download the app.
  • Free Apps: Generate revenue through ads, in-app purchases, or subscriptions.

Note: 93.9% of apps on the App Store and 97% on Google Play are free due to higher adoption rates.

docs.title: How Free Apps Make Money
docs.text:
• Advertisements: Earn revenue per click/view.
  • In-App Purchases: Users buy digital goods (e.g., coins, extra features).
  • Subscriptions: Recurring payments for exclusive content or features.

docs.title: Prototyping
docs.text: Having a prototype demonstrates commitment and makes it easier for investors to visualize your app.

docs.title: Low-Fidelity Prototypes
docs.text:
• Rough sketches or hand-drawn mockups
  • Useful for early-stage feedback

docs.title: High-Fidelity Prototypes
docs.text:
• Digital, interactive models using tools like Adobe XD or Sketch
  • Ideal for usability testing and investor presentations

docs.title: Creating a Pitch Deck
docs.text: Your pitch deck should be tailored to your funding stage (pre-seed, seed, Series A, etc.).

docs.title: Key Elements of a Strong Pitch Deck:
docs.text:
1. Introduction – Who you are and what your app is about
  2. Team – Background of your team members (if available)
  3. Problem – What problems your app solves
  4. Competition – Analysis of competitors and your unique advantages
  5. Product – How your app works
  6. Market – Data on market size and growth trends
  7. Revenue Model – How your app will make money
  8. Investment Needs – Budget breakdown
  9. Contact Information – How investors can reach you

docs.title: Pro Tip:
docs.text: Have an elevator pitch ready—a short version of your pitch that can be delivered in under a minute.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Investors seek confidence in the projects they fund. A well-prepared pitch deck, a solid monetization strategy, and a compelling prototype will significantly increase your chances of securing investment.

Make sure to: - Clearly define your problem and solution - Provide market data and competitive analysis - Demonstrate how your app will generate revenue - Present a polished pitch deck

With the right preparation, you can turn your app idea into a funded reality.

docs.title: 🔹 1. What is Inflation?
docs.text:
• Inflation is the rise in prices of goods and services over time.
  • It reduces your money's purchasing power.

Example: - Milk cost ₹50 last year → ₹60 now → 20% inflation.

docs.title: 🔹 2. What is Repo Rate?
docs.text:
• Repo Rate is the interest rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks.
  • RBI increases repo rate to control inflation.
  • RBI reduces repo rate to stimulate growth.

docs.title: 🔹 3. How Repo Rate Controls Inflation
docs.text: Phase Repo Rate Action Economic Impact Inflation rising RBI increases repo Loans costlier → Less borrowing → Demand drops Inflation falling RBI decreases repo Loans cheaper → Spending rises → Growth improves

docs.title: 🔹 4. Investing Based on Inflation & Repo Rate
🔶 PHASE 1: Inflation Rising, Repo Rate Rising
docs.text:
What Happens People spend less, equity volatile, gold rises ✅ Invest In Gold, Short-Term Debt Funds ❌ Avoid Long-Term Debt, Large Equity Exposure 💰 How to Invest SIP in debt, small SIP/lumpsum in gold

Example: Repo 6.5%, inflation rising → Gold ETF + Liquid Funds

docs.title: 🔴 PHASE 2: Inflation at Peak, Repo at Peak
docs.text:
What Happens Growth slows, interest highest, equity bottoms out ✅ Invest In Short-Term Debt, Start equity SIPs 🔄 Switch Start reducing gold 💰 How to Invest SIP in equity, shift some funds from gold to equity

Example: Gold ₹6,200, repo steady → Shift to equity SIPs, reduce gold holding

docs.title: 🟢 PHASE 3: Inflation Falling, Repo Starts Dropping
docs.text:
What Happens Growth returns, markets rise, bond prices rise ✅ Invest In Equity, Long-Term Debt Funds ❌ Avoid Fresh gold investments 💰 How to Invest Increase equity SIPs, invest lumpsum in long-term debt funds

Example: Inflation 4.5%, RBI cuts repo → Equity & bond funds rally

docs.title: ⚪ PHASE 4: Inflation & Repo Stable
docs.text:
What Happens Economy stable, best time for long-term investing ✅ Invest In Equity (flexi-cap, mid-cap), Hybrid Funds ⚖️ Keep Some debt + little gold (hedge) 💰 How to Invest Aggressive SIPs in equity, small lumpsum possible

Example: Inflation ~4%, repo stable → Midcap SIP + small debt & gold

docs.title: 🔹 5. Gold Investment Strategy
docs.text:
When to Buy Inflation rising, market uncertainty When to Sell Inflation peaks, repo likely to fall How to Buy Gold ETF, Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs)

Example: Buy ₹5,200 → Inflation peaks → Sell ₹6,000

docs.title: 🔹 6. Debt Fund Strategy
docs.text: Type Use When Benefit Short-Term Debt Repo rising / high Safe, stable interest Long-Term Debt Repo falling Bond price appreciation

docs.title: 🔹 7. Equity Strategy
docs.text: When to Avoid During inflation spike & repo hikes (Phase 1) When to Start When inflation peaks (Phase 2) When to Accelerate Repo cuts, growth returning (Phase 3 & 4)

docs.title: 🔹 8. Portfolio Allocation by Economic Phase
docs.text: Phase Equity Debt Funds Gold How to Invest 🟠 Rising Inflation 20–30% 50–60% (short) 20% SIP in debt, lumpsum in gold 🔴 Peak 30–40% 50% 10–20% Start equity SIPs, reduce gold 🟢 Falling Inflation 50–60% 30–40% (long) 5–10% Increase equity, long-term debt ⚪ Stable 70–80% 10–20% 5–10% Aggressive SIPs, diversified equity

docs.title: 🔹 9. SIP vs Lumpsum Strategy
docs.text: Situation Action Repo rising, inflation rising ✅ Use SIPs (safer entry) Repo at peak, inflation peaking 🔄 Partial lumpsum + SIP Repo falling, growth returning ✅ Big SIPs or staggered lumpsum Stable economy ✅ Aggressive SIPs for long term

docs.title: ✅ Final Tips
docs.text:
• 🏦 Track RBI repo updates every 2 months
  • 🪙 Hold 10–15% gold max as hedge, not return
  • 🛡️ Always keep Emergency Fund (3–6 months)
  • 🔄 Review portfolio every 6 months
  • 📱 Use apps like Groww, Coin, Zerodha, Kuvera for SIPs

docs.title: 1. C# data structure and algorithm
docs.text:
## Division of Data Types: 1. Value type 2. Reference type

A variable of value type directly contains the data, while a variable of reference type just store the reference of Data, which is located somewhere else.

Value type variable stores it's actual value directly in stack memory. Reference type variable store only reference here in stack, actuale value is located in heap memory.

  • Note: That's why two variable of Value type equal (==) if there data is equal while two variable of reference type will be equal if they referenc the same location

docs.title: 1. Value Type:
docs.text:
They are further divided into following categories:

  • Structs
    • Built-in value types
      • Integral numeric type
      • Floating-point numeric types
      • Boolean values
      • Unicode UTF-16 characters
    • Value tuples
    • User-defined struct types
  • Constants
  • Enumerations

docs.title: 1.1 Integral Number:
docs.text:
Supported integral types: - Byte (byte keyword) --> 8-bit unsigned - Sbyte (sbyte) --> 8-bit signed - Int16 (short) --> 16-bit signed - Uint16 (ushort) --> 16-bit unsigned - Int32 (int) --> 32-bit signed - UInt32 (unit) --> 32-bit unsigned - Int64 (long) --> 64-bit signed - UInt64 (ulong) --> 64-bit unsigned

Different Modes: 1. Decimal Mode No prefix needed, example: 45.

  1. HexaDecimal Mode Apply 0x or 0X as prefix , example: 0xff for 255.

  2. Binary Mode Apply 0b or 0B as prefix , example: 0b1101110 or 0b_0110_1110 for 110.

Example:

    int a = -20;
    byte b = 0x0f;
    uint c = 0b1101110;
    Console.WriteLine(a);     //-20
    Console.WriteLine(b);     // 15
    Console.WriteLine(c);     // 110

Remember that the default value for any built-in integral numeric type is zero.

docs.title: 1.2 Floating-point numbers:
docs.text:
It allow us to store floating-point values.You can use three floating-point numeric types:

  1. Single (float) using 32 bits – for example, 1.53f (f or F suffix)
  2. Double (double) using 64 bits – for example, 1.53 (no suffix or d/D suffix)
  3. Decimal (decimal) using 128 bits – for example, 1.53M (m or M suffix)

Example:

    float temperature = 36.6f;
    double reading = -4.5178923;
    decimal salary = 10000.47M;
    Console.WriteLine(temperature);     //  36.6
    Console.WriteLine(reading);         //  -4.5178923
    Console.WriteLine(salary);          //  10000.47

Remember that the default value for any floating-point numeric type is zero.

docs.title: 1.3 Boolean values:
docs.text:
Regarding Boolean values, you can use the Boolean type or the bool keyword. This makes it possible to store a logical value. It represents one of two values, namely true or false. The default value is false.

Example:

    bool isTrue = true;
    bool first = isTrue || false; // true
    bool second = isTrue && false; // false
    bool third = 50 > 10; // true

docs.title: 1.4 Unicode characters:
docs.text:
It is represented by the Char type or the char keyword. It represents a single Unicode character.

A char value can be specified using the following: - Character literal – for example, 'a' or 'M' - Unicode escape sequence, starting with \u – for example, '\u25cf' for ● - Hexadecimal escape sequence, starting with \x – for example, '\x107' for ć

Example:

    char letter = 'M';
    char bullet = '\u25cf';
    char special = '\x107';
    char Test = '\0';      //

The default value for a char value is \0 (U+0000).

docs.title: 1.5 Constants
docs.text:
It is worth noting that you can also define constant values. Each constant value is an immutable value that cannot be changed. Constant values can only be created from simple types. You can use the const keyword to create a constant value, as shown in the following line:

Example:


    const int DaysInWeek = 7;

docs.title: 1.6 Enumerations:
docs.text:
An enumeration (often called "enum") is a distinct data type that consists of a set of named values called enumerators. Enums are used to represent a collection of related constants in a type-safe way. For example enum CurrencyEnum { Pln, Usd, Eur };

The constants have automatically assigned values as integer numbers, starting with 0. This means that the Pln constant is equal to 0, while Eur is equal to 2. What’s more, the default value for the enumeration is 0, which means that it is Pln in this case.

Example:

    CurrencyEnum currency = CurrencyEnum.Pln;
    switch (currency)
    {
    case CurrencyEnum.Pln: /* Polish zloty */ break;
    case CurrencyEnum.Usd: /* American Dollar */ break;
    default: /* Euro */ break;
    }
    enum CurrencyEnum { Pln, Usd, Eur };

docs.title: 1.7 Value tuples
docs.text:
The value tuple type is represented by the System.ValueTuple type and is a lightweight data structure that allows you to group multiple data elements of specific types.

(int, int, double) result = Calculate(4, 8, 13);

docs.title: A. Dotnet Commands
docs.text:
• dotnet new nunit → Initialize an NUnit project in the selected folder.
  • dotnet new nunit -n "ProjectName" → Set the project name (internal name used in .csproj and namespace)
  • dotnet new nunit -o "ProjectName" -> Specifies the directory where Nunit project will be created.

ProjectName. - dotnet new classlib -n FrameworkDesign → Create a Class Library project named FrameworkDesign. - dotnet new specflowproject → Convert the selected folder into a SpecFlow project. - dotnet test --filter UnitTest1 → Run the UnitTest1 file. - dotnet test → Run all tests. - dotnet build → Build the project. - dotnet clean → Clean the project.

  • Adding a Reference Project: 
dotnet add reference ../ReferencProjName/ReferencProjName.csproj
  • Adding a Project to a Solution:

cd path\to\your\solution

docs.title: E. Build and Publish the Application
docs.text:
1. Build the Project: sh dotnet build

  2. This compiles your project and places the compiled binaries in the bin directory.

  3. Publish the Application: sh dotnet publish -c Release -o ./publish

  4. -c Release → Specifies Release mode. Use Debug for debugging, but Release is preferred for production.
  5. -o ./publish → Specifies the output directory where the published files will be stored.

docs.title: Git Commands cheatsheet
docs.text:
1. Open a Git Repository in VS Code To open any Git repository in VS Code, place the following keyword before https:
vscode.dev/
  1. Initialize a Git Repository
git init
  1. Configure Git Before making commits, configure your Git identity (name and email):
git config list    // display config details
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"
  1. Check Repository Status To see which files are staged, unstaged, or untracked:
git status
  1. Create a New Repository on the Command Line
echo "# pythonProjectwithRobot" >> README.md
git init                      //initialize the git to folder
git add README.md             //add README file to staging directoy
git commit -m "first commit"  // package all staging changes into a commit object(ID)
git branch -M main            // Move/rename a branch (-m for normaly, -M for forcely )
git remote add origin https://github.com/Abhikpt/pythonProjectwithRobot.git
git push -u origin main      //
  1. Stage Files for Commit Git add is used to add changes to the staging area.
git add <file1> <file2>  # Stage specific files
git add .                # Stage new and modified files without deleting
git add -a               # Stage all files to the staging area
git add -u               # Stage modified and deleted files
  1. Commit Changes Git saves the state of your project and assigns a unique identifier to the snapshot.
git commit -m "Your commit message"
  1. View Commit History
git log
  1. Create a Branch
git checkout -b <branch-name>
  1. Switch Between Branches
git checkout <branch-name>
  1. Merge Branches To merge changes from one branch into another (e.g., merging a feature branch into main):
git checkout main
git merge <branch-name>
  1. Push Changes to Remote Repository
git push origin <branch-name>
git push
  1. Pull Changes from Remote Repository
git pull origin <branch-name>
  1. Clone a Repository
git clone <repository-url>
  1. Revert Commit Changes This command will revert the latest commit (top commit):
git reset --hard HEAD^
  1. Review Changes Before Commit Always review changes before committing:
git diff
git diff --staged

  1. How do you find the longest substring without repeating characters in a string?

Steps: • Use two pointers (left and right) to maintain a sliding window. • Use a HashMap to store characters and their last seen indices. • If a duplicate character is found, move the left pointer to avoid repetition. • Keep track of the maximum length encountered.

 import java.util.HashMap;

public class LongestUniqueSubstring {
    public static int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
        HashMap<Character, Integer> charIndexMap = new HashMap<>();
        int maxLength = 0;
        int left = 0;

        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            char currentChar = s.charAt(right);

            // If character is repeated, update left pointer
            if (charIndexMap.containsKey(currentChar)) {
                left = Math.max(charIndexMap.get(currentChar) + 1, left);
            }

            // Store the latest index of the character
            charIndexMap.put(currentChar, right);

            // Update max length
            maxLength = Math.max(maxLength, right - left + 1);
        }

        return maxLength;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String str = "abcabcbb";
        System.out.println("Longest substring length: " + lengthOfLongestSubstring(str)); // Output: 3 ("abc")
    }
}

  1. Given a non-empty array of digits representing a non-negative integer, increment one to the integer. example:
Input Output [1,2,3] [1,2,4] [1,2,9] [1,3,0] [9,9,9] [1,0,0,0] 
  public static  int[] plusOne(int[] digits) {
    int n = digits.length;

    // Start from the end of the array  (check and retrun by incrementing 1 if any digit < 9)  [1,9,9] => [2,0,0]
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        if (digits[i] < 9) {
            digits[i]++;
            return digits;    // return out from code if < 9
        }
        digits[i] = 0;    // iterate for all digit if greater than 9
    }

    // If all digits were 9, we need to add a new digit at the beginning (9,9,9) => (1,0,0,0)
    int[] newNumber = new int[n + 1];
    newNumber[0] = 1;
    return newNumber;
}

docs.title: The System.Console Class
docs.text:
A static class in the System namespace for performing I/O operations in console applications.

Key Methods: - Write(value): Displays a value. - WriteLine(value): Displays a value and moves to the next line. - ReadLine(): Reads a string input. - ReadKey(): Waits for a key press. - Clear(): Clears the console.

docs.title: Variables in C
docs.text:
Variables are named memory locations used to store data during program execution.

Syntax:

data_type variable_name = value;

Rules: 1. No spaces or special characters (except _). 2. Cannot use keywords as variable names. 3. Must be declared before use.
