docs.title: Programming Model for Scalable Applications
docs.text:
• Used in most popular languages such as Java, Python, JavaScript, C++, etc.
  • The goal of OOP is to group data and its operations as a single unit called an "Object".

docs.title: Class
docs.text:
• A class is a blueprint for creating objects that encapsulate data and behaviors.
  • A class is a model of objects.
  • A class (a.k.a "type") represents the structure (list of fields and methods) of data you want to store in similar objects.
  • Objects are created based on a "Class".

Example:

class Car {
    string regNo;
    string carModel;
    int carYear;
}

docs.title: Key Points:
docs.text:
• A class represents the structure of data you want to store in an object.
  • It is not a collection of objects.
  • Classes can have only two types of access modifiers: public and internal.

Scenario: Imagine you are sitting at a table with two laptops, one Lenovo and one Dell: - You are an object of the Person class. - Lenovo and Dell are two objects of the Laptop class.

docs.title: Class Members:
docs.text:
1. Fields
  2. Methods
  3. Constructors
  4. Properties
  5. Events
  6. Delegates

docs.title: Concepts of Class:
docs.text:
1. Namespace: Organizes and groups related classes to avoid naming conflicts.
  2. Class Declaration: A blueprint for creating objects.
  3. Access Modifiers:
  4. public: Accessible anywhere.
  5. private: Accessible only within the class.
  6. protected: Accessible within the class and derived classes.
  7. Fields: Variables defined at the class level.
  8. Constants: Fixed values that cannot be modified.
  9. Constructor: Initializes fields or sets up the object.
  10. Properties: Provide controlled access to private fields.
  11. Events: Enable communication between objects.
  12. Methods: Perform operations or actions.
  13. Destructors: Cleanup when an object is destroyed.

Sample Code:

using System;

namespace OOPConceptsDemo
{
   public class MyClass
   {
      private string _name;
      public int Id;
      public const string Organization = "TechWorld";

      public string Name
      {
        get { return _name; }
        set { _name = value; }
      }

      public int Age { get; set; }

      public MyClass(int id, string name, int age)
      {
        Id = id;
        _name = name;
        Age = age;
      }

      public event Action OnDataUpdated;

      public void UpdateData(string newName, int newAge)
      {
        _name = newName;
        Age = newAge;
        OnDataUpdated?.Invoke();
      }

      public void DisplayInfo()
      {
        Console.WriteLine($"Id: {Id}, Name: {_name}, Age: {Age}, Organization: {Organization}");
      }

      ~MyClass()
      {
        Console.WriteLine("Object is being destroyed.");
      }
   }

   class Program
   {
      static void Main(string[] args)
      {
        MyClass person = new MyClass(1, "Alice", 25);
        person.OnDataUpdated += () => Console.WriteLine("Data has been updated!");
        person.DisplayInfo();
        person.UpdateData("Bob", 30);
        person.DisplayInfo();
      }
   }
}

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
• An object is a small unit (entity) in the program that represents a real-world person or thing.
  • A blueprint of a class.
  • Instance of a class.

  • Has behavior and properties.

  • Examples: You, Your laptop.

  • Any physical thing can be considered an object.
  • An object is an instance (example) of a "class".
  • Objects store a set of fields (details about the object).

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
• A method is a collection of statements to perform certain operations (processes or work), such as performing calculations, displaying output, or checking conditions.
  • A method should be a member (part) of a class.
  • Code statements are not allowed outside the class; they are allowed inside the method only.

Example:

class Car {
    int calculateEmi(int carPrice, int noOfMonths, int interestRate) {
        // Perform calculation here
        return emi;
    }
}

docs.title: Object & Class Association
docs.text:
• Objects store fields.
  • Objects associate with all methods of their class, meaning objects can call methods of their class.
  • A class declares a list of fields and defines a list of methods.

docs.title: Creating a Class
docs.text: Define the structure of the object.

docs.title: Creating an Object
docs.text:
1. Creating a Reference Variable: csharp ClassName referenceVariable;

  2. Create Object and Store its Reference: csharp referenceVariableName = new ClassName();

docs.title: Key Points to Remember
docs.text:
• An object is a programmatic representation of a person or thing.
  • All objects are created based on classes and stored in the 'heap'.
  • For each application execution, a new heap will be created (and only one).
  • All reference variables (local variables of methods) are stored in the stack. For each method call, a new stack will be created.
  • A method is a collection of statements to perform some operation or calculation.
  • A class supports two access modifiers: internal and public.
  • A class supports four modifiers: static, abstract, sealed, and partial.
  • Objects store actual data (group of fields) and can access methods of the class.
  • A reference variable stores the address of an (only one) object.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• Variables that are declared in the class and stored in the objects.
  • Fields are isolated for each object.

Example:

class Car {
    string regNo;
    string carModel;
    int carYear;
}

docs.title: Syntax of Field
docs.text: AccessModifier DataType FieldName;

docs.title: Access Modifiers of Fields
docs.text:
• Access Modifier (a.k.a. "Access Specifier" or "Visibility Modifier") specifies the accessibility of fields, determining where the fields can be accessed.
  • They provide security for the fields.

docs.title: Static Fields
docs.text:
• Static fields are stored outside the object.
  • Static fields are common to all objects of a class.

Example:

class BankAccount {
    long accountNumber;
    string accountHolderName;
    double currentBalance;
    static string bankName;
}

docs.title: Class Memory in Heap
docs.text: • Static Field: bankName: Bank of Dummyland

docs.title: Objects in Heap
docs.text:
• Object 1:
  • accountNumber: 1001
  • accountHolderName: Scott
  • currentBalance: 5000
  • Object 2:
  • accountNumber: 1002
  • accountHolderName: Bob
  • currentBalance: 6000

docs.title: Instance Fields vs Static Fields
docs.text: Aspect Instance Fields Static Fields Storage Stored in Objects Stored in Class's memory Related to Represents data related to objects Represents common data for all objects Declaration Declared without static keyword Declared with static keyword Accessible with Accessible with object (reference var) Accessible with class name only Memory Allocation Allocated separately for each object Allocated once for the entire program

docs.title: Constant Fields
docs.text:
• Constant fields are like static fields, common to all objects of the class.
  • The value of a constant field cannot be changed.
  • Constant fields are accessible with the class name (not with the object).
  • Constant fields are not stored in the object or memory; they are replaced with their value during compilation.
  • Constants must be initialized in-line with their declaration (with a literal value only).

Syntax:

AccessModifier const DataType FieldName = value;

docs.title: Readonly Fields
docs.text:
• Readonly fields are like instance fields, stored in every object individually.
  • The value of a readonly field cannot be changed.
  • Readonly fields are accessible with a reference variable (object).
  • Readonly fields must be initialized either "in-line with declaration" or "in the constructor".

Syntax:

AccessModifier readonly DataType FieldName = value;

docs.title: Key Points to Remember
docs.text:
• Fields are variables declared in the class but stored in objects.
  • Access modifiers of fields: private, protected, private protected, internal, protected internal, public.
  • Modifiers of fields: static, const, readonly.
  • Instance fields are individual for each object; static fields are common (one-time) for all objects.
  • Constants must be initialized along with the declaration; readonly fields must be initialized either "along with declaration" or in the "instance constructor".

docs.title: Member Variable
docs.text:
A member variable is a field inside a class but outside of a method.

```csharp internal class Pen { private string _brand = ""; // member variable private string _model = ""; // member variable

public Pen(string brand, string model)
{
   _brand = brand;
   _model = model;        
}

public void GetPenDetails()
{
   Console.WriteLine($"Pen {_brand} is created with model {_model}");
}

} ```

### Property - Properties are created to protect member variables. - They help access and control member variables from outside the class using get and set methods.

#### 1. Using get and set methods to change member variable values This approach includes additional logic for accessing or modifying the value.

Example: ```csharp private double _salary; public double Salary { get { return _salary * 0.95; } // Apply a 5% deduction set { _salary = value; } }

private string _password; public string Password { get { return "****"; } // Mask the password set { _password = value; } }

private string _name; public string Name { get { return _name; } set { if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value)) _name = value; } } ```

#### 2. Simplified get and set properties csharp public int Age { get; set; } public string Name { get; set; }

#### 3. Computed Property A computed property dynamically calculates its value based on other properties or fields.

Example: ```csharp public class AreaCalculator { public double Length { get; set; } public double Width { get; set; }

 // Computed property (read-only)
 public double GetArea
 {
    get { return Length * Width; }
 }

} ```

#### 1. Working with Read-Only Properties ```csharp using System;

namespace Coding.Exercise { public class MyClass { private readonly string _value;

    public string Value
    {
      get { return _value; }
    }

    public MyClass(string value)
    {
      _value = value;
    }
 }

 public class Exercise
 {
    public void PrintReadOnlyProperty()
    {
      MyClass obj = new MyClass("Read-Only Property Value");
      Console.WriteLine(obj.Value);
    }
 }

} ```

#### 2. Working with Write-Only Properties ```csharp public class MyClass { private string _password;

 public string Password
 {
    set { _password = value; }
 }

} ```

#### 3. Working with Keys (e.g., CustomerID) ```csharp public class Customer { public int CustomerID { get; private set; }

 public Customer(int id)
 {
    CustomerID = id;
 }

} ```

docs.title: Static Keyword
docs.text:
• Used to call a property or method without creating an object of the class.
  • Accessed using ClassName.MethodName or ClassName.PropertyName.
  • Cannot be called using an object of the class.
  • Declaring a member as static allows it to be accessed directly using the class name.
  • Static members include:
  • Static variables
  • Static methods
  • Static constructors
  • Static classes

### Constructor - A method with the same name as the class name. - Called when an object is instantiated. - Cannot be called again once the object is created. - Used to pass data to the class.

Types of Constructors: 1. Default Constructor: Constructor without parameters. 2. Custom Constructor: Constructor with parameters.

Example: ```csharp public class Customer { public string Name { get; set; } public string? Address { get; set; } public string? ContactNumber { get; set; }

 // Default constructor
 public Customer()
 {
    Name = "new customer";
    Address = "unknown";
    ContactNumber = "NA";    
 }

 // Custom constructor
 public Customer(string name, string address, string contact)
 {
    Name = name;
    Address = address;
    ContactNumber = contact;
 }

 // Custom constructor
 public Customer(string name)
 {
    Name = name;
 }

} ```

### Methods Methods are defined within a class to perform operations or actions.

#### Common Features: 1. Modifiers: - Access Modifiers: public, private, protected, internal, etc. - Behavior Modifiers: static, virtual, abstract, sealed, override.

  1. Parameters:

    • Optional Parameters: csharp public void Greet(string name = "Guest") { Console.WriteLine($"Hello, {name}!"); }
    • Params: csharp public void PrintNumbers(params int[] numbers) { foreach (var number in numbers) Console.WriteLine(number); }

  2. Return Types:

    • Can return any type, including void, primitive types, or complex types.
    • Can use Task or Task<T> for asynchronous methods.

### Named Parameters / Arguments - The named arguments enable us to specify an argument for a parameter by matching the argument with its name rather than with its position in the parameter list. - Useful when a method has many parameters or optional parameters.

Example: ```csharp public class EmployeeTest { string EmployeeName { get; set; } int EmployeeAge { get; set; }

 public void MethodWithOptionalParameter(string nam = "DefaultN", int age = 99)
 {   
    EmployeeName = nam;
    EmployeeAge = age;
 }

 public void GetEmployeDetails()
 {
    Console.WriteLine(EmployeeName + " has age: " + EmployeeAge);
 }

 public static void MethodPracticeMain()
 {
    EmployeeTest emp1 = new EmployeeTest();

    emp1.MethodWithOptionalParameter();  // Call method with optional parameter
    emp1.GetEmployeDetails();

    emp1.MethodWithOptionalParameter(age: 35, nam: "Abhishek");  // Call method with named parameter
    emp1.GetEmployeDetails();
 }

} ```

docs.title: Encapsulation:
docs.text:
• Protects important data inside a class.
  • Hides private or unwanted data from outside the class.

Access Modifiers: Access modifiers manage how classes and class members are accessed.

#### For Classes: 1. internal 2. public 3. private (only for nested classes)

  • private: Accessible only within the class.
  • public: Accessible from anywhere.
  • protected: Accessible within the class and derived classes.
  • internal: Accessible within the same assembly.
  • protected internal: Accessible within the same assembly or derived classes.
  • private protected: Accessible within the containing class or derived classes in the same assembly.

docs.title: Note:
docs.text:
• For classes we canuse only internal, public, and private Access modifier.
  • private acees modifier use only for nested classes

docs.title: Best practices:
docs.text:
1. Encapsulation: Use private methods to hide implementation details.
  2. Reusability: Use static or extension methods for utility functions.
  3. Simplicity: Avoid overusing modifiers like virtual unless necessary.
  4. Consistency: Use meaningful names and follow naming conventions (PascalCase).

docs.title: Collections in C
docs.text:
• Collections in C# are a set of predefined classes available in the System.Collections namespace. These classes provide more capabilities and flexibility than traditional arrays.
  • Collections are nothing but groups of records that can be treated as one logical unit.

docs.title: Examples:
docs.text:
• A Country Collection can contain items like CountryCode and CountryName.
  • A Product Collection might store ProductId and ProductName.
  • An Employee Collection could hold EmployeeId and EmployeeName.
  • A Book Collection might include ISBN and BookTitle.

docs.title: Key Features of Collections:
docs.text:
• Dynamic Size: Collections can grow or shrink dynamically as needed.
  • Insert/Remove at Any Position: You can insert or remove elements from anywhere in the collection.
  • Rich Functionality: Collections provide built-in methods to store, retrieve, update, delete, search, and sort objects.
  • Efficient and Reliable: They are well-tested and optimized for performance.

docs.title: Why Use Collections Instead of Arrays?
docs.text:
• Arrays have a fixed size, whereas collections can dynamically adjust.
  • Collections provide methods that make complex operations simpler.
  • Collections standardize the way objects are handled, promoting cleaner and more maintainable code.

docs.title: Common Operations:
docs.text:
With collections, you can easily: - Store and retrieve multiple objects - Search through elements - Sort and filter data - Perform batch operations like removing or updating elements

In simple terms, a collection in C# can be considered a more powerful and flexible form of array that is specifically designed to handle groups of objects efficiently.

docs.title: General Categories of Collections
docs.text: Collections are classified into 4 types.

docs.title: 1. Indexed-Based Collection
docs.text:
In indexed-based collections, an index is autogenerated while adding any element to the collection, such as arrays, lists, or ArrayLists. The index number can be used to identify the records.

Example of Country Collection:

Internal Index Country Code Country Name 0 IND India 1 AUT Austria 2 BLR Belarus 3 BTN Bhutan 4 JPN Japan 
Array[0] = "India";
List[1] = "AUT";

docs.title: 2. Key-Value Pair Collections
docs.text:
Key-value pair collections include Hashtable, Dictionary, and SortedList. In this type of collection, keys are used to identify elements instead of indexes.

Example of Country Collection:

Internal Index Country Code Country Name 0 IND India 1 AUT Austria 2 BLR Belarus 3 BTN Bhutan 4 JPN Japan 
Hashtable["IND"] = "India";

docs.title: 3. Prioritized Collections
docs.text:
Prioritized collections allow access to elements in a specific sequence. Examples include Stack and Queue.

  • Queue: First In First Out (FIFO)
  • Stack: Last In First Out (LIFO)

docs.title: 4. Specialized Collections
docs.text: Specialized collections are designed for specific purposes. For example, a HybridDictionary starts as a list and then becomes a hashtable.

docs.title: Why Use a Dictionary Instead of an Array?
docs.text:
Using a Dictionary<int, Employee> over a simple array of Employee objects offers several advantages:

  1. Key-based Access:
  2. A dictionary allows efficient access using a key.

  3. Example: csharp Employee emp = employees[2]; // Instantly get the employee with ID 2

  4. Handling Non-Sequential and Sparse Data:

  5. Dictionaries do not require contiguous or sequential keys, making them memory-efficient for sparse data.

  6. Flexibility in Modifying the Collection:

  7. Adding or removing entries in a dictionary is efficient and does not require shifting elements.

  8. Uniqueness of Keys:

  9. Ensures no two employees have the same ID, preventing data integrity issues.

  10. Performance:

  11. For large datasets, dictionaries offer significant performance advantages for lookups, additions, and deletions.

docs.title: Understanding Predicate and Delegate in C
What is a Delegate?
docs.text:
• A delegate is a type that represents references to methods with a specific signature.
  • It allows methods to be passed as parameters.

Example:

delegate void DisplayMessage(string message);

static void ShowMessage(string msg) {
    Console.WriteLine(msg);
}

DisplayMessage del = ShowMessage;
del("Hello, this is a delegate example!");

docs.title: What is a Predicate?
docs.text:
• A Predicate<T> is a built-in generic delegate that represents a method returning a bool (i.e., it checks a condition).

Example:

static bool IsEven(int number) {
    return number % 2 == 0;
}

List<int> numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 };
List<int> evenNumbers = numbers.FindAll(IsEven);
evenNumbers.ForEach(n => Console.WriteLine(n));

docs.title: Predicate Using Lambda Expression
docs.text:
• Instead of a separate method, you can use a lambda expression for Predicate<T>:
List<int> evenNumbers = numbers.FindAll(n => n % 2 == 0);

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

       String str = "swiss";

        // Call the function to find the index
        int index = firstNonRepeatingIndex(str);

        if (index != -1) {
            System.out.println("First non-repeating character is at index: " + index);
        } else {
            System.out.println("No unique character found.");
        }
    }

    public static int firstNonRepeatingIndex(String str) {
        // Step 1: Count the occurrences of each character
        HashMap<Character, Integer> charCount = new HashMap<>();

        // Traverse the string and populate the map with character counts
        for (char c : str.toCharArray()) {
            charCount.put(c, charCount.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);
        }

        // Step 2: Find the first character that appears only once
        for (int i = 0; i < str.length(); i++) {
            if (charCount.get(str.charAt(i)) == 1) {
                return i; // Return the index of the first unique character
            }
        }

        return -1; // Return -1 if no unique character is found
  }
}

  1. Reverse an Array:

Algorithm: 1. Step1: Create two variables named startIndex and endIndex and initialize values with 0 and (n-1) respectively. (n is the length of the array). 2. Step2: Swap the values of startIndex with endIndex and increment the value of startIndex by 1 (means +1) and decrement the value of endIndex by 1 (means -1). 3. Step3: Repeat Step2 until the startIndex value is less than the endIndex value. 4. Step4: Print the array as a reversed array.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

using System.Linq;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

namespace HelloWorld
{
  public class Program
  {
    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
      int[]   arry = {1,3,4,6,2,5,12}; 

      SwapElements(arry, 0, arry.Length-1); 

      Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", arry));      
    }  

    static void SwapElements(int[] arr, int startIndex, int endIndex)
        {
            while (startIndex < endIndex)
            {
                int temp = arr[startIndex];
                arr[startIndex] = arr[endIndex];
                arr[endIndex] = temp;
                startIndex++;
                endIndex--;
            }
        }
  }
}

  1. C# program to find two prime numbers whose sum equals the given prime number

• Check if the given number is prime. • Find two prime numbers (p1 and p2) such that: • p1+ p2 = given Prime Number • Print the pair of prime numbers.

Csharp:

using System;

class PrimeSumFinder
{
    // Function to check if a number is prime
    static bool IsPrime(int num)
    {
        if (num < 2) return false;
        for (int i = 2; i * i <= num; i++)
        {
            if (num % i == 0) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    // Function to find two prime numbers whose sum equals the given prime
    static void FindPrimeSum(int primeNumber)
    {
        if (!IsPrime(primeNumber))
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"{primeNumber} is not a prime number.");
            return;
        }

        bool found = false;

        for (int i = 2; i <= primeNumber / 2; i++)
        {
            int j = primeNumber - i;

            if (IsPrime(i) && IsPrime(j))
            {
                Console.WriteLine($"Prime numbers: {i} + {j} = {primeNumber}");
                found = true;
            }
        }

        if (!found)
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"No two prime numbers sum to {primeNumber}.");
        }
    }

    static void Main()
    {
        Console.Write("Enter a prime number: ");
        int primeNumber = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine());

        FindPrimeSum(primeNumber);
    }
}

docs.title: Four Dimensions of Software Architecture
docs.text: Dimension Description Example Structure Organization of system components. Microservices vs. Monolith. Behavior Interaction between components. REST APIs, Event-Driven Messaging. Quality Attributes Non-functional requirements (NFRs). Scalability, Security, Performance. Development & Evolution Maintainability and adaptability over time. CI/CD pipelines, Modular design.

docs.title: Architecture Decision vs. Design Principle
docs.text: Aspect Architecture Decision Design Principle Scope System-wide (e.g., database choice). Component-level (e.g., class structure). Impact Long-term, hard to change. Easier to refactor. Example "Use Kubernetes for orchestration." "Follow DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself)."

docs.title: First Law of Software Architecture
docs.text: "Everything in software architecture is a trade-off." Example: Choosing between consistency (ACID) vs. scalability (BASE) in databases.

docs.title: Architecture vs. Design Decision Criteria
docs.text: Criterion Architecture Design Scope Affects entire system. Limited to a component. Longevity Years. Weeks/months. Reversibility Costly to change. Easily refactored.

docs.title: Coupling vs. Cohesion
docs.text: Concept Goal Anti-Pattern Solution Coupling Minimize dependencies. ClassA directly modifies ClassB’s data. Use interfaces (Dependency Inversion). Cohesion Maximize relatedness. User class handles auth + logging. Split into AuthService and Logger.

docs.title: 1. SOLID Design Principles:
docs.text:
SOLID is a set of five design principles aimed at making software designs more maintainable, flexible, and scalable.

Principle Full Form Description S Single Responsibility Principle A class should have only one reason to change; it should have only one responsibility. O Open/Closed Principle Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. L Liskov Substitution Principle Subclasses should be substitutable for their base classes without altering program correctness. I Interface Segregation Principle A class should not be forced to implement interfaces it does not use. D Dependency Inversion Principle High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not on concrete implementations.

docs.title: 1.1 Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
docs.text: • A class should have only one responsibility (i.e., only one reason to change).

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
• Reduces complexity
  • Improves maintainability
  • Makes code easier to test

docs.title: How?
docs.text: • Split classes that handle multiple responsibilities into smaller, focused classes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
// ❌ Violation: Mixes user logic + file I/O
public class User
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public void SaveToFile(string path) { File.WriteAllText(path, Name); }
}

// ✅ Correct: Separated concerns
public class User { public string Name { get; set; } }
public class UserFileManager { public void SaveToFile(User user, string path) { ... } }

Explanation: The first class violates SRP by combining user data storage and file operations. The corrected version splits these into two classes, each with a single responsibility.

docs.title: 1.2 Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
docs.text: • Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
• Prevents breaking existing code
  • Encourages reusable, modular design

docs.title: How?
docs.text: • Use abstractions (interfaces, abstract classes) and inheritance.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
// ❌ Violation: Modifying existing code for new shapes
public class AreaCalculator
{
    public double CalculateArea(object shape)
    {
        if (shape is Rectangle r) return r.Width * r.Height;
        else if (shape is Circle c) return Math.PI * c.Radius * c.Radius;
        // Must modify for new shapes!
    }
}

// ✅ Correct: Extensible via interfaces
public interface IShape { double Area(); }
public class Rectangle : IShape { public double Width, Height; public double Area() => Width * Height; }
public class Circle : IShape { public double Radius; public double Area() => Math.PI * Radius * Radius; }

Explanation: The first example requires modifying AreaCalculator for new shapes. The second allows adding new shapes without changing existing code.

docs.title: 1.3 Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) —
docs.text:
• The Interface Segregation Principle is one of the SOLID principles of object-oriented design.
  • It helps you build clean, maintainable, and flexible systems.
  • It Says Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. i.e. Don’t create fat interfaces — instead, split them into smaller, more specific ones so that classes only implement what they really need.

docs.title: Bad Example(violate ISP)
docs.text:
//Below implementation violate ISP
    public interface IMachine
    {
        void Print(Document d);
        void Scan(Document d);
        void Fax(Document d);
    }

    public class OldPrinter : IMachine
    {
        public void Print(Document d) { /* OK */ }
        public void Scan(Document d) { throw new NotImplementedException(); }
        public void Fax(Document d) { throw new NotImplementedException(); }
    }
  • Here OldPrinter don't have capability to do Scan or Fax so we should not show option scan and Fax to user as per ISP.

docs.title: Good Example (Follows ISP):
docs.text:
// break down the interfaces
public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print(Document d);
}

public interface IScanner
{
    void Scan(Document d);
}

public interface IFax
{
    void Fax(Document d);
}


// implement only what needs:

public class SimplePrinter : IPrinter
{
    public void Print(Document d) => Console.WriteLine("Printing...");
}

public class MultiFunctionPrinter : IPrinter, IScanner, IFax
{
    public void Print(Document d) => Console.WriteLine("Printing...");
    public void Scan(Document d) => Console.WriteLine("Scanning...");
    public void Fax(Document d) => Console.WriteLine("Faxing...");
}
  • Now each class implements only the feature it actually supports.
  • See the full Source code here

## Dependency Inversion and Dependency Injection Principles

docs.title: 🔗 Dependency
docs.text:
• A dependency means one class relies on another to perform a function.
  • This leads to tight coupling, where changing one class may affect the other.

docs.title: 🔄 Coupling
docs.text:
• Coupling measures how closely two classes or modules are connected.
  • High coupling makes the system rigid and difficult to test or extend.
  • Good software design promotes loose coupling for flexibility and maintainability.

docs.title: 💡 Dependency Injection (DI)
docs.text:
• A design pattern used to reduce coupling between classes.
  • Instead of a class instantiating its dependencies, they are injected from outside.
  • Follows the Dependency Inversion Principle: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.

docs.title: 🧱 DI Involves 3 Types of Classes
docs.text:
Type Description Client Class The dependent class that uses a service (e.g., EmployeeBusinessLogic). Service Class The class that provides the service or functionality (e.g., EmployeeDbService). Injector Class Supplies the service class object to the client (can be the Main() method).

We use interfaces to define the contract of the service. This allows the client to remain unaware of which concrete implementation (e.g., SQL, Oracle, Excel) is being used.

docs.title: 1. Constructor Injection
docs.text:
• The Injector Injects the Dependency Object (i.e. Service Object) into the Client Class through the Client Class Constructor.
  • Ensures the class gets its required dependency at initialization.
public class EmployeeBusinessLogic
{
    private readonly IEmployeeDbService _employeeDbService;

    public EmployeeBusinessLogic(IEmployeeDbService employeeDbService)
    {
        _employeeDbService = employeeDbService;
    }

    public List<Employee> GetAllEmployees() => _employeeDbService.SelectAllEmployees();
}

// Usage in Main
var service = new EmployeeDbService();
var logic = new EmployeeBusinessLogic(service);
logic.GetAllEmployees();

docs.title: 2. Property Injection (Setter Injection)
docs.text:
• When the Injector Injects the Dependency Object (i.e. Service Object) into the Client Class through the public Property of the Client Class, then it is called Property Dependency Injection. This is also called the Setter Injection.
  • Useful when the dependency is optional or needs to change.
public class EmployeeBusinessLogic
{
    public IEmployeeDbService EmployeeDataService { private get; set; }

    public List<Employee> GetAllEmployees()
    {
        return EmployeeDataService.SelectAllEmployees();
    }
}

// Usage
var logic = new EmployeeBusinessLogic();
logic.EmployeeDataService = new EmployeeDbService();
var employees = logic.GetAllEmployees();

docs.title: 3. Method Injection
docs.text:
• When the Injector Injects the Dependency Object (i.e. Service Object) into the Client Class through a public Method of the Client Class, then it is called Method Dependency Injection.
  • Flexible but may make method signatures more verbose.
public class EmployeeBusinessLogic
{
    public List<Employee> GetAllEmployees(IEmployeeDbService employeeService)
    {
        return employeeService.SelectAllEmployees();
    }
}

// Usage
var logic = new EmployeeBusinessLogic();
var employees = logic.GetAllEmployees(new EmployeeDbService());

docs.title: ✅ Benefits of Dependency Injection
docs.text: Benefit Description Loose Coupling Promotes separation of concerns and easier testing. Increased Testability Makes it easy to use mock or stub objects for unit testing. Better Maintainability Changes in one class require fewer (or no) changes in others. Easier Extensibility New implementations can be introduced without modifying client code. Adheres to SOLID Principles Encourages Single Responsibility and Dependency Inversion.

docs.title: 2. Creational Patterns
docs.text:
All of the creational patterns deal with ways to create instances of objects. This is important because your program should not depend on how objects are created and arranged. In C#, of course, the simplest way to create an instance of an object is by using the new operator.

Fred fred1 = new Fred(); //instance of Fred class

docs.title: 2.1 Singleton Pattern
docs.text: The Singleton pattern ensures that a class has only one instance and provides a global access point to it. [control object creation]

docs.title: Why:
docs.text: Ensures controlled access to a single resource (e.g., logger, configuration, caching). Saves memory and improves performance when one object is enough. Useful when only one instance is logically required (e.g., PrintSpooler, Database Connection Manager).

docs.title: Required Elements / Steps:
docs.text: Element Explanation In Your Example Private Constructor Prevents external classes from creating new instances using new. private Logger() { } Static Instance Variable Holds the single instance of the class. private static Logger _instance; Public Static Property Provides global access to the instance with lazy initialization. public static Logger Instance Thread Safety (optional) Ensures only one thread can create the instance in multi-threaded environments. lock (_lock) Sealed Class (C# specific) Prevents inheritance to protect Singleton behavior. public sealed class Logger

docs.title: How:
docs.text: Private constructor Static field to hold the instance Public static method/property to access the instance Thread safety (for multithreading scenarios)

docs.title: Example with Thread-safe
docs.text:
public sealed class Logger
{
    private static Logger _instance;
    private static readonly object _lock = new();

    private Logger() { } // To Prevent external instantiation from other classes

    public static Logger Instance
    {
        get
        {
            lock (_lock) // Thread-safe
            {
                return _instance ??= new Logger();
            }
        }
    }

    public void Log(string message) => Console.WriteLine(message);
}

Explanation: - lock ensures thread safety. - sealed prevents inheritance. - Usage: Logger.Instance.Log("Hello");

docs.title: 2.2 Factory Method Pattern
docs.text: • Defines an interface for creating objects but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
• Decouples client code from concrete classes
  • Simplifies adding new product types

docs.title: How?
docs.text:
1. Creating Product Interface ICreditCard with method signature GetCardType, GetTotalAmount, GetAnaualCharge.
  2. Creating Concrete Products (MoneyBack, Titanium, and Platinum) and implement interface methods
  3. Creating Interface Creator (ICreditCardFactory). The Abstract Creator declares the factory method, which returns an object of type Product.
  4. Creating Concrete Creator(PlatinumFactory, MoneyBackFactory, and TitaniumFactory) that implement Creator interface methods.
  5. Consuming the Factory Method in the Client Code.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
public abstract class Document
{
    public List<Page> Pages { get; } = new();
    public abstract void CreatePages(); // Factory method
}

public class Resume : Document
{
    public override void CreatePages()
    {
        Pages.Add(new SkillsPage());
        Pages.Add(new EducationPage());
    }
}

public class Report : Document
{
    public override void CreatePages()
    {
        Pages.Add(new SummaryPage());
        Pages.Add(new ConclusionPage());
    }
}

Explanation: - Resume and Report are concrete creators that implement CreatePages(). - Clients use Document without knowing the concrete page types.

docs.title: 2.3 Factory Design Pattern
docs.text: The Factory Design Pattern is a creational design pattern that provides an interface for creating objects in a superclass, but allows subclasses to alter the type of objects that will be created. This pattern is particularly useful when the exact type of the object to be created is not known until runtime.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
• Decouples client code from concrete classes, so that no need to modify the client code if changing Product details, removing the product etc.
  • Simplifies adding new product types
  • Allows clients to use interface/abstraction, not concrete classes.
  • Object creation logic is centralized in the factory.
  • Promotes the Open/Closed Principle (Open for extension, closed for modification).

docs.title: ✅ 1. Required Elements / Steps in Factory Design Pattern
docs.text: Element Explanation In Your Code Product Interface Defines the contract (common methods/properties) that all product types implement. ICreditCard Concrete Products Specific implementations of the product interface. MoneyBack, Platinum, Gold Factory Class (Creator) Contains logic to instantiate appropriate concrete class based on input/conditions. CreditCardFactory.GetCreditCard() Client Code Consumes the product interface, unaware of which concrete class was created. Main_ConsumeProducts() method

docs.title: How?
docs.text: • Define a Creator abstract class with a factory method.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
namespace CSHARPCONCEPTS.CreationalDesignPattern;
public class FactoryDesignPattern
{
    // created product interface to expose operation a credit card should have
    public interface ICreditCard
    {
        string GetCardType();
        int GetCreditLimit();
    }

    // created concrete/Product classes (MoneyBack, Platinum, Gold) implementing the CreditCard interface
    public class MoneyBack : ICreditCard
    {
        public string GetCardType()
        {
            return "Money Back Credit Card";
        }

        public int GetCreditLimit()
        {
            return 50000;
        }
    }

    public class Platinum : ICreditCard
    {
        public string GetCardType()
        {
            return "Platinum Credit Card";
        }

        public int GetCreditLimit()
        {
            return 100000;
        }
    }

    // created a factory class to generate the object of concrete classes based on the information provided
    public class CreditCardFactory
    {
        public static ICreditCard GetCreditCard(string cardType)
        {
            if (cardType.Equals("MoneyBack"))
            {
                return new MoneyBack();
            }
            else if (cardType.Equals("Platinum"))
            {
                return new Platinum();
            }           
            else
            {
                Console.WriteLine("Invalid Card Type");
                return null;
            }
        }
    }    

    // consume the product classes inside the client code
    public static void Main_ConsumeProducts()
    {
        string cardType = "MoneyBack"; // input from UI
        ICreditCard creditCard = CreditCardFactory.GetCreditCard(cardType);

        // Displaying the card details
        if (creditCard != null)
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Card Type: " + creditCard.GetCardType());
            Console.WriteLine("Credit Limit: " + creditCard.GetCreditLimit());
            Console.WriteLine("Annual Charge: " + creditCard.GetAnnualCharge());
        }
        else
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Invalid Card Type");
        }
    } 
}

Explanation: - MoneyBack and Platinu are concrete creators that implement cardlimit and getCardType. - Clients use CreditCardFactory without knowing the concrete page types.

docs.title: 🚀 3. Benefits of Factory Design Pattern
docs.text: Benefit Explanation ✅ Loose Coupling Client code is not directly dependent on concrete classes. ✅ Centralized Object Creation Factory handles object creation, reducing duplication and improving maintainability. ✅ Improved Scalability New product types (e.g., TitaniumCard) can be added with minimal changes to client code. ✅ Easy Testing and Maintenance You can mock the interface ICreditCard during unit testing. ✅ Encapsulation of Complexity Complex object creation logic (e.g., configuration, dependencies) is hidden in the factory. ✅ Run-Time Decision Making Objects can be created based on input/configuration received at runtime (like UI input).

docs.title: 3.1 Observer Pattern
docs.text: • Defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all dependents are notified.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
• Enables event-driven systems
  • Loose coupling between subjects and observers

docs.title: How?
docs.text: • Use IObservable<T>/IObserver<T> or custom interfaces.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
public class WeatherStation : IObservable<WeatherData>
{
    private List<IObserver<WeatherData>> _observers = new();

    public IDisposable Subscribe(IObserver<WeatherData> observer)
    {
        _observers.Add(observer);
        return new Unsubscriber(_observers, observer);
    }

    public void UpdateWeather(WeatherData data)
    {
        foreach (var observer in _observers)
            observer.OnNext(data);
    }
}

public class Display : IObserver<WeatherData>
{
    public void OnNext(WeatherData data) => Console.WriteLine($"Temp: {data.Temperature}°C");
}

Explanation: - WeatherStation (subject) notifies Display (observer) when weather changes. - Built-in IObservable<T> handles subscriptions.

docs.text:
Concept Category Key Benefit SRP SOLID Reduces complexity Singleton Creational Global access to a single instance Observer Behavioral Decouples event sources and handlers

docs.title: Mobile testing
docs.text: 🏠 Home

docs.title: ✨ Overview
docs.text: • Cypress is a web UI automation tool for modern JavaScript applications (e.g., React, Angular, Vue).

docs.title: 🔹 Features
docs.text:
1. Time Travel – View DOM snapshots by hovering over each step.
  2. Debuggability – Debug in the same browser window without re-running.
  3. Automatic Waits – Cypress waits for DOM and elements automatically.
  4. Consistent Results – Runs yield consistent behavior.
  5. Auto Screenshots & Videos – Automatically captures on failure.
  6. Cross-Browser Testing – Runs on Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Electron.

docs.title: ❌ Limitations
docs.text:
1. Cannot automate Windows or mobile native apps.
  2. Limited community support.
  3. Only JavaScript/TypeScript supported.
  4. Difficult file read/write operations.
  5. Limited 3rd-party reporting integration.

docs.title: ⚙ Setup and Project Configuration
docs.text:
1. Ensure Node.js is installed:
   npm -v
````

2. Initialize Node Project (if `package.json` not present):

```bash
    npm init
  1. Install project dependencies:
    npm install
  1. Install Cypress:
    npm install cypress --save-dev
  1. Launch Cypress:

bash npx cypress open

  • Select E2E Component Testing
  • Choose browser (e.g., Chrome)

  • Create or choose test file

  • Write test cases in VS Code:

  • Go to cypress/e2e/

  • Rename and update the file

  • Run Tests:

bash npx cypress open # Headed mode with test runner npx cypress run # Headless mode npx cypress run --headed # CLI headed mode npx cypress run --spec <path> # Specific spec file npx cypress run --spec <path> --browser edge --headed

docs.title: Test Format
docs.text: • Spec File (.cy.ts) → describe() block → it() blocks

docs.title: Sample
docs.text:
describe("Home Page", () => {
  it("The h1 contains the correct text", () => {
    cy.visit("http://localhost:3000")
    cy.get("h1").should("contain", "Welcome")
  })
})

docs.title: Important Methods
docs.text:
• describe("Test Suite Name", callback)
  • it("Test Case Description", callback)
  • .only() → Run specific test or suite
  • .eq(index) → Selects element by index from matched set

docs.title: ✨ Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use data-cy attributes for selectors.
  • Keep reusable functions in commands.ts.
  • Add plugins in support/e2e.ts.
  • Use .only() and .skip() for selective execution.
  • Structure folders clearly: e2e/, fixtures/, support/.

docs.title: Cypress vs Traditional Tools
docs.text:
Feature Selenium/Protractor Cypress Execution Outside browser (via drivers) Inside browser Speed Slower (network hops) Very fast DOM Access Indirect via driver Direct Network Control Limited Full control, mock support Auto-Wait Manual Built-in Browser Support Wide Chrome, Firefox, Electron, Edge
  • Traditional tools use browser drivers and communicate over a network.
  • Cypress executes test code inside the browser, eliminating drivers and network latency.
  • Advantages: faster execution, direct DOM control, network interception, auto-waiting, real-time execution.

docs.title: Test Capabilities
docs.text:
• Unit, Integration, and End-to-End (E2E) testing.
  • Fits multiple SDLC stages.

docs.title: Supported Browsers
docs.text: • Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Electron (default, lightweight Chromium).

docs.title: Cypress Components
docs.text:
• Test Runner: UI for running/debugging tests, time-travel, live reload.
  • Dashboard Service: Optional cloud service for historical results, videos, error logs.

docs.title: 🛠️ Cypress Installation & Setup
docs.text:
1. Install Node.js: Download from official site.
    • Verify: node -v, npm -v
  2. Set NODE_HOME (Windows): Add Node.js path to environment variables.
  3. Install VS Code: Recommended editor.
  4. Create Project Folder: mkdir cypress-automation && cd cypress-automation
  5. Initialize npm Project: npm init -y
  6. Install Cypress: npm install cypress --save-dev
  7. Run Cypress: npx cypress open (creates /cypress folder structure)
  8. Share Setup: Commit package.json and package-lock.json; teammates run npm install.

docs.title: 🧪 Cypress Test Runner & CLI
docs.text:
• Open Test Runner: npx cypress open or ./node_modules/.bin/cypress open
  • Folder Structure: /cypress/ with downloads/, fixtures/, support/, cypress.config.js
  • Test Types: E2E or Component; select browser (Chrome, Firefox, Electron).
  • Write Tests: Place .js spec files in configured folder.
  • Configure Spec Path: In cypress.config.js, set specPattern.
  • Run Tests: Click spec file in UI; see step-by-step execution, DOM snapshots, time-travel debugging.

docs.title: CLI Commands
docs.text: Task Command Open Cypress GUI npx cypress open Run all tests headless npx cypress run Run specific test file npx cypress run --spec "path/to/file.js" Run in headed mode npx cypress run --headed Run in Chrome npx cypress run --browser chrome Run in Edge npx cypress run --browser edge Run in Firefox npx cypress run --browser firefox

docs.title: 🗂️ Cypress Project Structure
docs.text: Folder/File Purpose fixtures/ Test data (JSON files) integration/ Test scripts/spec files plugins/ Event handlers (rarely used) support/ Custom commands, utilities node_modules/ Cypress dependencies cypress.config.js Global configuration

docs.title: Example cypress.config.js
docs.text:
const { defineConfig } = require('cypress')

module.exports = defineConfig({
  e2e: {
     specPattern: 'cypress/integration/examples/*.js',
     screenshotsFolder: 'cypress/failures/screenshots',
     videosFolder: 'cypress/failures/videos',
     viewportWidth: 1000,
     viewportHeight: 660
  }
})

docs.title: 🔍 Element Identification & CSS Selectors
docs.text:
• Cypress supports CSS selectors (not XPath).
  • Inspect elements using browser DevTools.
  • Selector strategies:
  • #idName (ID)
  • .className (Class)
  • tag.class or tag#id (Tag + Class/ID)
  • [attribute="value"] (Attribute)
  • parent child (Hierarchy)
  • Validate selectors in DevTools: document.querySelector('selector')
  • Use Cypress Selector Playground for suggestions.
  • Locate elements: cy.get('css_selector')

docs.title: Why Use Cucumber BDD?
docs.text:
• Gherkin syntax (Given-When-Then) for readable, collaborative test cases.
  • Stakeholders can review scenarios.

docs.title: Setup Steps
docs.text:
1. Install Plugin: npm install --save-dev cypress-cucumber-preprocessor
  2. VS Code Extension: Install "Cucumber (Gherkin) Full Support".
  3. Create Feature File: Place .feature files in cypress/e2e/BDD/.
  4. Step Definitions: Create JS files in matching folders (e.g., BDD/ecommerce/ecommerceStepDef.js).

docs.title: Example Gherkin Syntax
docs.text:

const { defineConfig } = require("cypress");

docs.title: Introduction to Testing
docs.text: Software testing is a critical process in software development that aims to identify defects or errors in a software application before it is released to end-users. It ensures that the software meets the specified requirements and functions as expected. Effective testing improves software quality, reliability, and user satisfaction.

docs.title: Test Case Design Techniques in Software Testing
docs.text: Test case design techniques are essential for planning, designing, and implementing tests for software applications. These techniques can be classified into three major groups:

docs.title: a. Specification-Based or Black-Box Techniques
docs.text:
Black-box testing focuses on testing the software system based on its functional requirements and specifications without any knowledge of the underlying code or system structure.

  1. Boundary Value Analysis (BVA):

    • BVA identifies errors at the input domain's boundary.
    • Example: Testing a text box that requires the user to enter a number between 1 and 10.
    • Boundary values: 1 and 10.
    • Test values: Min (1), Min+1 (2), Min-1 (0), Max (10), Max+1 (11), Max-1 (9).

  2. Equivalence Partitioning (EP):

    • EP reduces the number of test cases by partitioning input data into classes where all elements within a partition are expected to be treated the same by the software.
    • Example: If a program requires an input of numbers between 1 and 100, an EP test would include a range of values, such as 1-50 and 51-100, and numbers outside that range, such as -1 or 101.

  3. Decision Table Testing:

    • This technique involves designing test cases based on decision tables, which represent different combinations of inputs and their corresponding outputs based on various conditions and scenarios, adhering to business rules.

  4. Use Case Testing:

    • This involves designing test cases to execute different business scenarios and end-user functionalities.

docs.title: 🔹 Example:
docs.text: Condition A Condition B Action 1 Action 2 T T ✓ T F ✓ F T ✓ F F ✗ ✗ 4.  State Transition Diagrams (STD): * Developers use STDs to test software with a finite number of states of different types. A set of rules that define the response to various inputs guides the transition from one state to another.

docs.title: b. Structure-Based or White-Box Techniques
docs.text:
White-box testing involves testing the internal structures or components of software applications. In this approach, the tests interact with the code directly.

  1. Statement Testing and Coverage:

    • This technique involves executing all the executable statements in the source code at least once.

  2. Decision Testing/Branch Coverage:

    • Also known as branch coverage, this technique validates all the branches in the code by executing each possible branch from each decision point at least once.

  3. Multiple Condition Testing:

    • This technique aims to test different combinations of conditions to achieve 100% coverage.

docs.title: c. Experience-Based Techniques
docs.text:
Experience-based testing relies on the testers’ skill, intuition, and experience to anticipate potential errors in the product.

  1. Error Guessing:

    • This testing technique relies on the testers’ skill, intuition, and experience to anticipate potential errors in the product.

  2. Exploratory Testing:

    • This technique is used to test applications without any formal documentation.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text: Automation is a word for applications where reduce human efforts. There are include business process automation (BPA), IT automation, personal applications, business related applications, E-commerce applications such as home automation, and more.

docs.title: Automation Testing
docs.text: Automation testing involves using specialized tools and scripts to execute test cases, compare actual outcomes with expected results, and report findings. It helps reduce manual effort, improve accuracy, and accelerate the testing process.

docs.title: Types of Automation Testing
docs.text:
1. Web Application Testing Automation testing for web applications ensures that the functionality, performance, and compatibility of the application work as expected across different browsers and platforms.

    • Tools Used: Selenium, Cypress, Playwright, TestCafe.

  2. API Testing API testing focuses on verifying the functionality, reliability, and performance of APIs. It ensures that APIs return the correct responses for various requests and handle edge cases effectively.

    • Tools Used: Postman, RestAssured, SoapUI, Karate.

  3. Mobile Application Testing Mobile testing ensures that mobile applications function correctly on various devices, operating systems, and screen sizes. It includes functional, performance, and compatibility testing.

    • Tools Used: Appium, Espresso, XCUITest, TestComplete.

docs.title: Benefits of Automation Testing
docs.text:
• Faster execution of repetitive test cases.
  • Improved test coverage and accuracy.
  • Early detection of defects.
  • Cost and time efficiency in the long run.

Automation testing is a critical component of modern software development, enabling teams to deliver high-quality applications efficiently.

docs.title: 1. Send a GET Request and Validate Status Code
docs.text:
Explanation: RestAssured allows sending requests and validating responses in a single line.

given()
.when()
    .get("https://api.example.com/users")
.then()
    .statusCode(200);

docs.title: 2. Send a POST Request to Create a New User
docs.text:
Explanation: Sends a JSON body with user data and checks if the response returns a 201 Created status.

given()
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .body("{\"name\": \"John\", \"job\": \"Engineer\"}")
.when()
    .post("https://api.example.com/users")
.then()
    .statusCode(201);

docs.title: 3. Validate a JSON Response Field
docs.text:
Explanation: Validates the email field in the JSON response.

.then()
    .body("data.email", equalTo("john@example.com"));

docs.title: 4. Add Headers in a Request
docs.text:
Explanation: Adds Content-Type and Authorization headers.

given()
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer your_token");

docs.title: 5. Validate API Response Time
docs.text:
Explanation: Checks if the response time is less than 2 seconds.

.then()
    .time(lessThan(2000L));

docs.title: 6. Verify JSON Field Presence
docs.text:
Explanation: Checks if the response JSON has a "data" key.

.then()
    .body("$", hasKey("data"));

docs.title: 7. Send a PUT Request
docs.text:
Explanation: Sends a PUT request to update user information.

given()
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .body("{\"name\": \"John\", \"job\": \"Manager\"}")
.when()
    .put("https://api.example.com/users/2")
.then()
    .statusCode(200);

docs.title: 8. Handle Pagination
docs.text:
Explanation: Keeps requesting pages until there are no more records.

int page = 1;
while (true) {
    Response response = given()
        .queryParam("page", page++)
    .when()
        .get("https://api.example.com/users");

    List<Object> users = response.jsonPath().getList("data");
    if (users.isEmpty()) break;
    users.forEach(System.out::println);
}

docs.title: 9. Verify JSON Array Size
docs.text:
Explanation: Checks if the data array has exactly six items.

.then()
    .body("data.size()", equalTo(6));

docs.title: 10. Extract Specific Data from JSON
docs.text:
Explanation: Uses jsonPath() to extract values.

String email = response.jsonPath().getString("data.email");

docs.title: 11. Send a DELETE Request
docs.text:
Explanation: Removes a user resource, expecting status 204 No Content.

.when()
    .delete("https://api.example.com/users/2")
.then()
    .statusCode(204);

docs.title: 12. Validate Specific Header in Response
docs.text:
Explanation: Checks if Content-Type header matches expected value.

.then()
    .header("Content-Type", equalTo("application/json; charset=utf-8"));

docs.title: 13. Handle Query Parameters
docs.text:
Explanation: Passes query parameters like page=2.

given()
    .queryParam("page", 2);

docs.title: 14. Handle Basic Authentication
docs.text:
Explanation: Provides username and password for basic auth.

given()
    .auth().basic("username", "password");

docs.title: 15. Send a PATCH Request for Partial Update
docs.text:
Explanation: Updates only specific fields without overwriting all data.

given()
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .body("{\"job\": \"Architect\"}")
.when()
    .patch("https://api.example.com/users/2")
.then()
    .statusCode(200);

docs.title: 16. Add Multiple Query Parameters
docs.text:
Explanation: Adds multiple query parameters using repeated queryParam() calls.

given()
    .queryParam("page", 1)
    .queryParam("limit", 10);

docs.title: 17. Check for Non-Null JSON Path Value
docs.text:
Explanation: Ensures data.email is not null.

.then()
    .body("data.email", notNullValue());

docs.title: 18. Send Form Parameters
docs.text:
Explanation: Used when content type is application/x-www-form-urlencoded.

given()
    .contentType("application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
    .formParam("username", "john")
    .formParam("password", "1234");

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
1. Install Playwright CLI :

  1. Initialize Playwright:
    playwright install
  1. Create an directory
    dotnet new Nunit -n PlaywrightPractice
  1. Go to created directory: 
    cd PlaywrightPractice
  1. Add dependencies in project:
    dotnet add package Microsoft.Playwright
    playwright install
    playwright install msedge  # Optional for Edge channel

  1. Write your Script

  2. Run the test

    dotnet run
  1. Basic Syntax: ```csharp using Microsoft.Playwright;

class Program { public static async Task Main() { using var playwright = await Playwright.CreateAsync(); var browser = await playwright.Chromium.LaunchAsync(new BrowserTypeLaunchOptions { Headless = false }); var context = await browser.NewContextAsync(); var page = await context.NewPageAsync(); await page.GotoAsync("https://example.com"); await page.ScreenshotAsync(new PageScreenshotOptions { Path = "screenshot.png" }); await browser.CloseAsync(); } } ```

docs.title: 👨‍💻 Base Class Structure Example
docs.text:
public class PlaywrightBase
{
    protected IPlaywright _playwright;
    protected IBrowser _browser;
    protected IBrowserContext _context;
    protected IPage _page;

    public async Task StartAsync(bool headless = true)
    {
        _playwright = await Playwright.CreateAsync();
        _browser = await _playwright.Chromium.LaunchAsync(new BrowserTypeLaunchOptions {
            Channel = "msedge",
            Headless = headless
        });
        _context = await _browser.NewContextAsync();
        _page = await _context.NewPageAsync();
    }

    public async Task StopAsync()
    {
        await _context?.CloseAsync();
        await _browser?.CloseAsync();
        _playwright?.Dispose();
    }
}

docs.title: 📘 Data-Driven Testing with Playwright + NUnit (C#)
docs.text: This document covers how to perform data-driven testing using Playwright with C# and NUnit, along with multiple ways to provide test data.

docs.title: ✅ What is Data-Driven Testing?
docs.text: Data-driven testing allows running the same test logic with multiple sets of input data. This helps in increasing test coverage with less code duplication.

docs.title: ✅ Basic Example Using [TestCase]
docs.text:
Use when you have small static test data.

[TestCase("user1", "pass1")]
[TestCase("user2", "pass2")]
public void LoginTest(string username, string password)
{
    // Your Playwright test logic here
}

docs.title: ✅ Using [TestCaseSource] with Static Property
docs.text:
public static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> LoginData =>
    new List<TestCaseData>
    {
        new TestCaseData("user1", "pass1"),
        new TestCaseData("user2", "pass2")
    };

[Test, TestCaseSource(typeof(MyDataClass), nameof(MyDataClass.LoginData))]
public void LoginTest(string username, string password)
{
    // Test logic
}
  • typeof(MyDataClass) tells NUnit where to find the data.
  • nameof(MyDataClass.LoginData) specifies the exact member to use.

docs.title: ✅ Using Static Method as Data Source
docs.text:
Allows conditional logic or dynamic data creation.

public static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> GetLoginData()
{
    yield return new TestCaseData("user1", "pass1");
    yield return new TestCaseData("user2", "pass2");
}

[Test, TestCaseSource(typeof(MyDataClass), nameof(MyDataClass.GetLoginData))]

  { "username": "user1", "password": "pass1" },

docs.title: 🔹 C# Code
docs.text:
public static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> LoginDataFromJson()
{
    var json = File.ReadAllText("testdata.json");
    var users = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject<List<LoginModel>>(json);
    foreach (var user in users)
    {
        yield return new TestCaseData(user.Username, user.Password);
    }
}

docs.title: ✅ Using Environment Variables or GitHub Secrets
docs.text:
Good for use in CI/CD pipelines to avoid hardcoding sensitive data.

public static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> SecretsData()
{
    var username = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("USERNAME");
    var password = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("PASSWORD");
    yield return new TestCaseData(username, password);
}

docs.title: ✅ Reading from Database
docs.text:
Use when test data is stored in a DB:

public static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> LoginDataFromDb()
{
    using var conn = new SqlConnection("connection-string");
    conn.Open();
    var cmd = new SqlCommand("SELECT username, password FROM users", conn);
    var reader = cmd.ExecuteReader();

    while (reader.Read())
    {
        yield return new TestCaseData(reader["username"], reader["password"]);
    }
}

docs.title: NUnit Framework
docs.text: NUnit is a popular unit-testing framework for .NET.

docs.title: Features of NUnit Framework
docs.text:
• Multiple Asserts: Assert.Multiple() allows raising multiple assertions in a single test.
  • Parallel Execution: Supports parallelism at test method and test fixture levels.
  • Test-Driven Development (TDD): Facilitates TDD practices.
  • Author Attribution: Enables multiple authors to be attributed to the code.
  • Annotations: Uses annotations to speed up test development and execution.

docs.title: Execution Flow of NUnit Test
docs.text: A basic process flow of a Selenium Testing program with NUnit involves the following steps:

docs.title: Annotations in NUnit
docs.text:
• TestFixture:
    • A class-level attribute indicating that the class contains NUnit test methods.
    • Can only be placed on classes, not methods.
    • Supports parameterized TestFixtures via constructors.
    • If no arguments are provided, the class must have a default constructor.
    • Multiple TestFixture attributes can be used on a single class.
    • TestFixture attribute can be inherited.
  • TestCase:
    • Marks a method as a test method.
    • Passes arguments/parameters to the test method.
    • TestCase attribute properties:
      • Parameterized: [TestCase(20)] - Passes arguments/parameters to the method.
      • ExpectedResult: [TestCase(parameter, ExpectedResult = false)] - Validates the return type of the method.
      • Author: [TestCase(Author = "Abhishek")] - Assigns the author of the test case.

docs.title: NUnit Assert Examples
docs.text: Assert methods compare the actual result with the expected result. If they match, the test case passes; otherwise, it fails.

docs.title: Constraint Model
docs.text: NUnit provides a constraint model using the That method to improve test method readability. The That method applies constraints to the actual value.

docs.title: Helper Classes
docs.text:
Helper classes provide constraints for assertions:

  • Is
  • Has
  • Contains
  • Does
  • Throws

docs.title: Page Object Model (POM) in Selenium C#
docs.text: POM is a design pattern used to improve the maintainability of Selenium test code.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Separation of test code and page-specific code (locators, layout).
  • Centralized repository for page services/operations.

docs.title: Example of Login using POM and without POM
Login Feature without POM
docs.text:
public class Login
{
    public void testLogin()
    {
        // Fill login data on sign-in page
        driver.findElement(By.name("user_name")).sendKeys("userName");
        driver.findElement(By.name("password")).sendKeys("my supersecret password");
        driver.findElement(By.name("sign-in")).click();

        // Verify h1 tag is "Hello userName" after login
        driver.findElement(By.tagName("h1")).isDisplayed();
        assertThat(driver.findElement(By.tagName("h1")).getText(), is ("Hello userName"));
    }
}

docs.title: Problems with this approach:
docs.text:
• No separation between test methods and locators.
  • Locators are scattered across multiple tests.

docs.title: Login Feature with POM
docs.text:
• Create a directory containing page classes/page objects.
  • Create another directory containing test scripts/actual code implementation.
public class SignInPage
{
    protected WebDriver driver;
    private By usernameBy = By.name("user_name");
    private By passwordBy = By.name("password");
    private By signinBy = By.name("sign_in");

    public SignInPage(WebDriver driver)
    {
        this.driver = driver;
        if (!driver.getTitle().equals("Sign In Page"))
        {
            throw new IllegalStateException("This is not Sign In Page, current page is: " + driver.getCurrentUrl());
        }
    }

    public HomePage loginValidUser(string userName, string password)
    {
        driver.findElement(usernameBy).sendKeys(userName);
        driver.findElement(passwordBy).sendKeys(password);
        driver.findElement(signinBy).click();
        return new HomePage(driver);
    }
}

docs.title: Page Factory in Selenium C#
docs.text:
• Page Factory is a design pattern that enhances POM.
  • It Initializes page class elements without FindElement.
  • It Uses @FindsBy annotation to find elements.
  • PageFactory.InitElements() must be use to initializes web elements.

docs.title: Example Pagefactory:
docs.text:
using OpenQA.Selenium;
using SeleniumExtras.PageObjects;

public class LoginPage
{
    private readonly IWebDriver driver;

    public LoginPage(IWebDriver driver)
    {
        this.driver = driver;
        PageFactory.InitElements(driver, this);
    }

    [FindsBy(How = How.Id, Using = "username")]
    public IWebElement UsernameInput { get; set; }

    [FindsBy(How = How.Id, Using = "password")]
    public IWebElement PasswordInput { get; set; }

    [FindsBy(How = How.Id, Using = "loginButton")]
    public IWebElement LoginButton { get; set; }

    public void Login(string username, string password)
    {
        UsernameInput.SendKeys(username);
        PasswordInput.SendKeys(password);
        LoginButton.Click();
    }
}

docs.title: Data-Driven Testing in C#
docs.text: Data-driven testing involves running the same test multiple times with different sets of input data.

docs.title: Techniques for Data-Driven Testing
docs.text:
1. NUnit Attributes and Parameterized Methods:

    • Using [TestCase()] attribute to provide parameters for test methods.

  2. Product Model:

    • When dealing with complex product details, using a product model as a parameter can simplify test data management.
    • Instead of passing individual parameters, pass a model object containing all relevant data.

  3. Random Data Generation using AutoFixture:

    • Install the AutoFixture.NUnit3 NuGet package.
    • Use the [AutoData] attribute to generate random data for test parameters.

  4. SpecFlow Scenario Outline:

    • Use SpecFlow's scenario outlines to supply data from feature files.

  5. External Data Files (CSV, Excel, etc.):

    • Read test data from external files like CSV or Excel.

  6. Passing Complete Models:

    • Create a model, assign values to its properties, and pass the model to the test method to create requests.

  7. Using appsettings.json:

    • Extract configuration data from appsettings.json files.

docs.title: Working with Config file (appsettings.json)
docs.text:
Steps to read test settings from a configuration file:

  1. Create appsettings.json:

    • Create a JSON file named appsettings.json to store configuration data.

  2. Configure appsettings.json to Copy to Bin Directory:

    • Option 1 (Visual Studio):
      • Select the file in Solution Explorer.
      • Go to Properties.
      • Set "Copy to Output Directory" to "Copy always".

    • Option 2 (Project File):

      • Add the following configuration to your project file (.csproj):

      xml <ItemGroup> <None Update="appsettings.json"> <CopyToOutputDirectory>Always</CopyToOutputDirectory> </None> </ItemGroup>

  3. Create ConfigReader.cs:

    • Create a ConfigReader.cs file to read data from appsettings.json and map it to a model (e.g., TestSetting).

  4. Access Data:

    • Use the ConfigReader.ReadConfig() method to access the data.

    csharp TestSetting testSetting = ConfigReader.ReadConfig();

//ConfigReader.cs
using System;
using System.IO;
using System.Reflection;
using System.Text;
using LWASpecflow.Utilities;
using Newtonsoft.Json;

namespace LWASpecflow.Utilities;

  public class ConfigReader
  {

        public static TestSetting ReadConfig()
          {
              string accessFile = File.ReadAllText(GetprojectDir() + "/appsettings.json") ;   
              return JsonConvert.DeserializeObject<TestSetting>(accessFile) ;
          }

      public static string GetprojectDir()
      {
          String biDirctorty = Environment.CurrentDirectory; 
           String workingDir = Directory.GetParent(biDirctorty).Parent.Parent.ToString();
          string projectDir  =  workingDir + "\\Utilities";
          return projectDir;
      }
  }

docs.title: Reading Test Data from External Sources (Excel, CSV, etc.)
docs.text:
Data-driven testing involves reading test data from external sources.

  • Data sources include:

    • Excel files
    • CSV files
    • Databases
    • XML files
    • ODBC sources

  • Reading Data from Database:

    • Use TestContext object and [DataSource] attribute.

  • Data-Driven Testing with XML:

    • Read test data from XML files.

  • Data-Driven Testing with CSV:

    • Read test data from CSV files.

  • Configuration File Data Source:

    • Use configuration files to define data sources.

  • Reading and Writing Excel using OLEDB:

    • OLEDB is a COM-based API for accessing data from various sources (databases, spreadsheets, text files).

    Implementation Steps:

    1. Create an Excel file named ProductTestData with a sheet named AddProduct.
    2. Ensure file fields match the ProductData model.
    3. Create an ExcelOperation class.

    ExcelOperation.cs:

    ```csharp using System.Data.OleDb; using FrameworkDesign.Config; using FrameWorkDesign.DataSet; using Dapper;

    namespace FrameWorkDesign.Utilities;

    public class ExcelOperation { private readonly OleDbCommand connection;

    public static string TestDataFileConnection()
{
    var fileLocation = ConfigReader.ReadConfig().ProductDataFile;
    var conString = string.Format(@"Provider=Microsoft.ACE.OLEDB.12.0;Data Source = {0}; Extended Properties=Excel 12.0;", fileLocation);
    return conString;
}

public static ProductData GetTestData(string testName)
{
    var connection = new OleDbConnection(TestDataFileConnection());
    connection.Open();
    var query = string.Format("select * from [AddProduct$] where keyName = '{0}'", testName);
    var value = connection.Query<ProductData>(query).FirstOrDefault();
    connection.Close();
    return value;
}

    } ```

    1. Access the retrieved data:

    csharp ProductData productData = ExcelOperation.GetTestData("YourTestName"); // Access productData properties

docs.title: AutoFixture (Random Data Generation)
docs.text:
AutoFixture is a .NET library for automatically generating test data.

  1. Creating Objects Automatically:

    csharp var fixture = new Fixture(); var person = fixture.Create<Person>();

  2. Creating Lists or Collections:

    csharp var people = fixture.CreateMany<Person>(5);

  3. Customizing Object Creation:

    csharp var fixture = new Fixture(); var person = fixture.Build<Person>() .With(p => p.Name, "John Doe") .Create();

  4. Auto-Data Tests with xUnit:

    ```csharp using AutoFixture.Xunit2;

    public class PersonTests { [Theory, AutoData] public void Person_HasValidProperties(Person person) { Assert.NotNull(person.Name); Assert.InRange(person.Age, 0, 120); } } ```

docs.title: Parallel Testing and Reporting in C#
Parallelizable
docs.text:
When running multiple tests in parallel, WebDriver instances can interfere with each other, leading to data mismatches. To prevent this, we use thread-safe WebDriver instances.

  • Thread Safety:

    • Initialize WebDriver using ThreadLocal<IWebDriver>: csharp public ThreadLocal<IWebDriver> driver = new ThreadLocal<IWebDriver>();
    • Access the WebDriver instance using driver.Value.

  • Parallelization Annotations:

    1. Parallel Data Sets within a Test Method:

      • [Parallelizable(ParallelScope.All)]
      • Place before the test method to run all data sets in parallel.

    2. Parallel Test Methods within a Class:

      • [Parallelizable(ParallelScope.Children)]
      • Place before the class to run all test methods in the class in parallel.

    3. Parallel Test Files within a Project:

      • [Parallelizable(ParallelScope.Self)]
      • Place before the class in each test file to run all test files in the project in parallel.
